piezas.titulo: Occupational Therapy in LGBTQ + Affirming Primary Care: Referral, Intervention, and Outcomes.
piezas.resumenOriginal: ImportanceLGBTQ + clients experience healthcare barriers that may shape daily routines, health management, and participation. Little is known about occupational therapy referral pathways and outcomes in LGBTQ + affirming primary care.ObjectiveTo describe referral characteristics, occupational performance concerns, intervention focus, and client-reported outcomes among LGBTQ + clients referred to occupational therapy.DesignRetrospective pilot program evaluation using clinical documentation and outcome data from July 2025 through March 2026, with a June 2026 analysis cutoff.SettingTwo Midwestern primary care settings where occupational therapy screening and referral processes were developed; ongoing intervention occurred through outpatient occupational therapy.ParticipantsThirty-nine referred clients were included in descriptive analyses; 38 received intervention beyond evaluation; 21 had complete baseline and follow-up Canadian Occupational Performance Measure data.InterventionIndividualized outpatient occupational therapy focused on client-identified concerns.Outcomes and MeasuresReferral and treatment characteristics, occupational performance concerns, coded occupational focus, and Canadian Occupational Performance Measure Performance and Satisfaction ratings.ResultsCommon concerns included instrumental activities of daily living (94.9%), health management/self-management (92.3%), activities of daily living (82.1%), and work or school participation (82.1%). The most common primary intervention focus was health management and chronic condition self-management (65.8%). Among participants with outcome data, COPM Performance scores improved by 2.29 points and Satisfaction scores improved by 2.58 points.Conclusions and RelevanceOccupational therapy may support LGBTQ + clients referred from primary care by addressing needs related to health management, routines, self-care, and participation through individualized outpatient intervention. Prospective multisite research is needed.

piezas.titulo: Gentle touch modulates late spinal and cortical somatosensory responses without detectable changes in spinal component N13 and nociceptive flexion reflex amplitude
piezas.resumenOriginal: Affective and gentle touch have been associated with changes in pain and somatosensory perception, but it remains unclear whether these effects reflect early spinal gating or later cortical and descending processes. We investigated whether gentle touch with CT-optimal characteristics modulates spinal and cortical somatosensory and nociceptive processing across three experiments. Experiment 1 compared the sural-nerve nociceptive flexion reflex (NFR; RIII) in the leg while the forearm received no touch, vibration, robot-delivered brushing, or human-delivered stroking. Experiment 2 compared somatosensory evoked potentials (SEPs) across the same four conditions. Experiment 3 compared robot-delivered brushing with no touch, including additional trials to improve sensitivity to spinal SEP modulations. RIII amplitudes and spinal (N13, P22) and cortical (N20, P25, N30, P45, N60, P150) SEP components were analyzed. Gentle touch modulated neither the heterosegmental NFR nor the segmental N13, arguing against inhibition of early afferent transmission within or beyond the touched segment. However, Experiment 3 revealed modulation of the P22 spinal component, suggesting that gentle touch may influence spinal processing through supraspinal feedback mechanisms. At the cortical level, both robot- and human-delivered gentle touch attenuated the N60 and P150 components relative to vibration and no-touch conditions, indicating modulation of later stages of somatosensory processing consistent with attentional and cognitive influences. These findings suggest that CT-optimal gentle touch does not act through direct segmental inhibition of incoming sensory signals, but instead modulates later spinal and cortical processing, likely through descending influences. This study provides a multilevel neurophysiological framework for understanding how affective touch shapes sensory processing.

destilado.texto: Gentle touch no altera el reflejo flexor nociceptivo ni el componente N13 de la médula espinal. Sin embargo, reduce los componentes corticales N60 y P150, modula el componente de spinal processing P22 y sugiere que gentle touch actúa mediante retroalimentación descendente, ofreciendo una vía potencial para intervenir el dolor.

piezas.titulo: Engram: Multi-Stage Memory for Agentic Tuning of Heterogeneous Models
piezas.resumenOriginal: arXiv:2611.28356v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents can now tune neural networks, yet without cross-session memory they spend costly trials rediscovering known lessons. Reuse is difficult because production models differ in architecture, training setup and inference budget. We present Engram, a memory system that links past trial outcomes with the hypotheses and rationale behind them and assesses whether this evidence applies to the current model. An online agent curates evidence at the decision points where it is needed: Initial Guidance supplies validated lessons at the start, Session Retrieval supplies related past sessions before each batch of hypotheses is generated, and Trial Candidate Review checks each trial candidate against matching past trials. Between sessions, an offline agent distills validated lessons, making the memory self-improving. On two ads models, Engram reaches the 32-trial result of a no-memory control with 47% fewer trials and also ends with a better model on average.

piezas.titulo: Virtual Reality Interventions Involving Occupational Therapists in Adults with Neurological Conditions: A Scoping Review.
piezas.resumenOriginal: Background/objectives Virtual reality (VR) is increasingly being incorporated into neurorehabilitation to support functional training and participation in meaningful activities. However, the characteristics of VR interventions involving occupational therapists remain insufficiently described. This scoping review aimed to describe VR interventions involving occupational therapists for adults with neurological conditions. Methods A scoping review was conducted following the PRISMA-ScR guidance. A systematic search was performed in PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, Embase and CENTRAL. Randomized controlled trials and quasi-experimental studies examining VR interventions for adults with neurological conditions and involving at least one occupational therapist were included. Study selection and data charting were independently performed by two reviewers. Results Seventy-one studies were included, of which 58 were randomized controlled trials. Most studies included 50 participants or fewer ( n = 62), and the median study-level age was 58.6 years. Stroke was the neurological condition investigated exclusively in most studies ( n = 60), and motor, sensory, and other body-function outcomes were the most frequently assessed ( n = 65). Activities of daily living (ADL) and occupational performance were assessed in 48 studies, whereas participation was assessed in only 6. Interventions lasted a median of 4.8 weeks and non-immersive VR predominated ( n = 62). Occupational therapists were most commonly involved in intervention or rehabilitation delivery, supervision, or configuration. Conclusions VR interventions involving occupational therapists were predominantly non-immersive, focused on adults with stroke, with occupational therapist involvement most often comprising direct intervention or rehabilitation delivery, supervision, or configuration. Outcomes mainly addressed motor, sensory, and other body functions and ADL/occupational performance, while participation was rarely assessed, highlighting important gaps for future research. Future studies should broaden the range of technologies and neurological conditions, place greater emphasis on participation, and report the specific role of occupational therapists more clearly.

piezas.titulo: Building an agentic stack in Envoy: routing models, tokens, and MCP
piezas.resumenOriginal: At Google Cloud, we believe the next generation of AI and agentic systems must be built on open, battle-tested foundations. Envoy, an open-source edge and service proxy designed for cloud-native applications, has already transformed microservices and modern cloud networking, powering everything from Google Cloud’s Application Load Balancers to the Agent Substrate dataplane on Google Kubernetes Engine. Now, Envoy is uniquely positioned to become the open standard for AI traffic, MCP tooling, and agent-to-agent communication. Earlier this year, we presented the technical case for Envoy networking in the agentic AI era , examining how autonomous AI agents fundamentally challenge traditional Layer 7 networking assumptions. Unlike microservices, autonomous agent workloads choose who they communicate with. In addition, their routing attributes live deep within request bodies, with their traffic governed by token budgets as well as request rates, and their multi-turn reasoning loops requiring stateful session affinity and strict tool execution boundaries. At Google Cloud, we have been working hard to develop Envoy for the agentic era. Read on for a closer look at how Envoy has evolved to better support autonomous agents, giving developers the performance and portability of an open-source ecosystem, backed by enterprise security and scalability. Why autonomous agents challenge traditional L7 proxies Over the past decade, Envoy became the industry standard for cloud-native traffic management by operating cleanly at Layer 4 (TCP/UDP connection management) and Layer 7 (URI, method, and header-based routing). Autonomous agents introduce two higher-order protocol layers: Layer 8 (agentic interaction protocols): such as LLM APIs , Anthropic’s Model Context Protocol (MCP) and Google’s Agent2Agent (A2A) , running over JSON-RPC 2.0 or gRPC. Critical policy attributes—such as tools/call , tool_name: "execute_sql" , or model: "gemini-1.5-pro" —are serialized inside the request payload. Layer 9 (agent framework interfaces): Coordination frameworks such as UCP, AP2, and Google Cloud’s Agent Development Kit, where multi-turn workflows produce dynamic token consumption and non-linear execution graphs. Fronting these workloads with traditional L7 proxies creates four major architectural challenges: Payload blindness: Nearly all LLM traffic shares the same paths (such as /v1/chat/completions ), so a header-based proxy cannot distinguish between a low-cost query and an expensive 500,000-token prompt, or one model from another. Request rate limiting fallacy: One request per minute with a massive context window can use more accelerator compute and memory bandwidth than dozens of short queries, and agent loops can burn through budgets unnoticed. Stateless load balancing: Each turn of an agent's conversation should go back to the server that already remembers it. Traditional load balancers send it to whichever server is next, so the model has to start over for every turn, this wastes time and GPUs. Ungoverned tool execution: Agents query databases, execute code in sandboxes, and call third-party APIs. Without inline inspection of MCP tool calls, organizations risk prompt injection, data exfiltration, and runaway billing loops. The core pillars of Envoy’s agentic stack To address these challenges, Envoy provides capabilities that turn the network into an active governance layer: Core Pillar Operational Functionality 1. Native body parser Payload blindness: Read request bodies, not just headers. Line-rate payload normalization across OpenAI, Anthropic, and Gemini schemas with SSE stream handling. 2. Tokenomics engine Request-rate fallacy: Count tokens, not just requests. Pre-inference token estimation, tokens per minute (TPM) / tokens per day (TPD) rate limiting 3. Model & MCP routing Stateless load balancing: Keep agent sessions on the right servers Endpoint Picker (EPP) model dispatch, KV-cache prefix affinity, MCP Stateless support. 4. AI security guardrails Ungoverned tool execution: Policy tool calls. Inline policy, decision point (ext_proc) callouts for guardrails: Model Armor, ShieldGemma, and data loss prevention. 1. Native wire-format body parsing and transcoding Client applications often get locked into specific model APIs. For example, client code built for OpenAI's schema cannot communicate with Anthropic's endpoints or Google’s Gemini without client-side translation layers. To help, Envoy ecosystem includes native body parsers that normalize requests across diverse model families, providing: Client abstraction: Upstream applications send a standardized schema. Envoy inspects the JSON payload at line-rate, extracts the target model, and dynamically transcodes the request into the downstream provider's native format. No application code changes: Switching from an external commercial model to a self-hosted open-source model (such as Gemma or Llama on vLLM) requires only an Envoy configuration update. Application code remains unchanged. Streaming token extraction: Envoy parses server-sent events (SSE) response streams in real time, capturing token counts from usage chunks while maintaining ultra-low time-to-first-token latency. 2. Tokenomics engine: token-aware traffic management In AI networking, tokens are the fundamental unit of capacity . Envoy replaces coarse request counters with token-aware traffic management features such as: Token rate limiting: Enforces tokens per minute (TPM) and tokens per day (TPD) limits per tenant, project, or model. Pre-inference throttling: Envoy estimates input tokens from request payload bytes and extracts actual token usage from LLM responses to record in a quota database, rejecting subsequent over-quota requests with an HTTP 429 before they reach the inference cluster. Runaway loop protection: Autonomous agents can enter recursive reasoning loops. By tracking cumulative token consumption and message counts per session or agent ID, Envoy throttles multi-turn sessions once an agent exceeds its assigned budget. 3. Model routing and Model Context Protocol (MCP) support Envoy manages traffic for both downstream model backends and outbound tool calls, with: KV-cache prefix affinity: Using the Kubernetes Gateway API Inference Extensions and Endpoint Picker (EPP), Envoy routes prompts sharing identical system instructions to the GPU worker currently holding that cache in memory, reducing latency. Model retry and fallback: If a primary model returns a 429 status code or fails, Envoy automatically retries or redirects the request to a secondary model pool with zero client interruption. MCP tool routing: For MCP agents, Envoy routes requests via JSON-RPC 2.0 bodies and HTTP headers. Per the 2026-07-28 MCP specification , Envoy uses Mcp-Method and Mcp-Name headers for zero-body-parsing routing to backend servers. Backends reject header-body mismatches with an HTTP 400 / -32020 (HeaderMismatch) error to prevent tampering. 4. AI security guardrails Inline safety filtering cannot come at the expense of network throughput. To prevent this, Envoy provides security callouts: Using standardized external processing ( ext_proc ), Envoy connects to dedicated policy decision engines — such as Google Cloud’s Model Armor, ShieldGemma, or local classifiers — to detect prompt injections and sensitive data leaks with minimal latency overhead. High-density infrastructure: Envoy and Agent Substrate In enterprise production environments, agents frequently spend time idle between user queries or long-running tool executions. Running hundreds of thousands of idle agents in dedicated containers or virtual machines can create prohibitive infrastructure costs. Envoy pairs directly with high-density execution runtimes like Agent Substrate to provide: Scale-to-zero traffic steering: Agent Substrate uses lightweight isolation runtimes (such as Cloud Hypervisor, microVMs and gVisor application sandboxes) that can suspend and resume in milliseconds. When traffic arrives for a suspended agent, Envoy buffers the initial packet while signaling the runtime to resume the instance, completing the end-to-end resume in milliseconds. Egress perimeter defense: Envoy functions as both an ingress and egress gateway for agent environments, routing the inbound traffic and restricting outbound network calls to verified domains and preventing untrusted autonomous code from reaching unauthorized endpoints. Getting started Envoy has evolved into an intelligent, extensible networking layer designed specifically for the unique demands of multi-agent architectures. To begin building with the agentic stack in Envoy: Explore the code: Review the Envoy proxy and Agent Router implementations on Github and examine the open-source sample configurations. Join the community: Participate in CNCF, Gateway API , and Kubernetes AI Gateway Working Group to collaborate on standardized inference APIs, MCP routing specifications, and token management conventions.

piezas.titulo: Why Your RAG Pipeline, Not Your LLM, Is Causing Hallucinations
piezas.resumenOriginal: Every time a large language model produces a confidently wrong answer, the industry reaches for the same word: hallucination. It’s a tidy label. It frames the failure as a mysterious, almost biological quirk of the model itself, as if the AI briefly lost touch with reality and there’s not much anyone can do about it except wait for a better model. That framing is convenient for model vendors. It is much less convenient for the truth. In production systems, especially retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipelines, which is how most enterprise AI actually gets deployed the majority of “hallucinations” I’ve seen traced back to something far less mysterious: bad data engineering. Stale indexes. Naive chunking. Missing metadata. Broken retrieval ranking. Silent ingestion failures. None of that is a model problem. All of it gets blamed on the model anyway. If you work in data engineering and you’ve been treating hallucination as someone else’s problem a model-layer issue for the ML team to solve it’s worth looking closer. There’s a good chance the fix lives in your pipeline, not their weights.

piezas.resumenOriginal: It’s that time of the year when the November Thoughtworks Technology Radar appears. Again my colleagues have taken a sweep of the technologies that our teams have used in the field, and pulled together a summary of what’s popped up in the last six months. It’s been a busy half-year, one that again has been dominated by AI, and that’s reflected in the many AI blips on the radar. The mass of blips makes it hard to develop a coherent story around trends, but Chris Ford has done a fine job of the writing the accompanying article on macro trends . One team of passionate people experimenting with agents can make almost anything work. They share a context, a credit card and a mental model. They review each other’s work because they sit together, and they know what to check and how much latitude to give the coding agent. Two hundred people, though, cannot work that way. The moment agentic AI becomes an operating model rather than a pilot, a second layer of problems appears: How is context shared between teams? What’s the token bill? How do we deal with increased review demands? What’s the agent allowed to reach, read and change? And who’s now responsible for the harness everyone depends on? Experience so far suggests that the questions that enterprises face are about: shared context, token cost, cognitive load, security, and platform building. While these issues are distinct, they are not separate, so strategies to answer them must take all of them into account. I also echo Chris in reminding us that however impressive these tools are, we must remember that while we have to rethink systems and workflows to utilize these technologies, they should be built to serve humans - and we should all benefit from its bounty. ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ Ben Thompson’s Stratechery newsletter reflects on the recent election’s impact on data centers . I watch a lot of sports, and particularly this fall, watched a lot of baseball. My Milwaukee Brewers — excuse me, my World Champion Milwaukee Brewers — demanded my full attention, which also meant I saw a lot of campaign ads, and by far the most common topic, at least here in Wisconsin, was data centers. Moreover, it was never entirely clear which way it cut politically: both parties were anti-data center, accusing their opponent of being the opposite. He points out that this opposition is recent, and tied to a shift in focus from the internet and streaming movies to AI: you know, the technology that in the best case scenario is going to take everyone’s jobs, and in the worst case scenario end the human race. There’s going to be a lot said about how Democratic officials will be at the heart of blocking data center building, but as his point above about campaign ads illustrates, the opposition to data centers is (at least at the moment) a bi-partisan opposition. He follows up with “ten takes” from these consequences. The big beneficiaries of this opposition to building data centers will be those who own the data centers that have already been built. The opposition will reduce supply of tokens, meaning that token costs will go up, thus increasing the profits for those who already have their token generators plugged in and humming. There’s also benefits to those who aren’t constrained by the need to build more big data centers. Other countries aren’t affected by a change in US policy, China is the most talked-about case here, but it’s not the only country that may benefit from a drop in US data center building. Apple may also benefit, if it means more AI work is pushed to edge devices that are their territory, in addition to having not sunk so many dollars into AI-specific investments. To his analysis, I’ll add that this may also have a somewhat counter-intuitive effect on regulation, and corporate attitudes to it. The common expectation is that businesses are opposed to government regulation, since that interferes with their free pursuit of profit. That’s true to an extent, but it’s quite common to see established businesses lobby (quietly) in favor of regulation that acts as a barrier to new competitors. So I wouldn’t be at all surprised to see companies that have already built data centers to be pushing for regulations that impede or prevent new ones from being built. ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ I’ve been a long-time fan of Hadley Wickham, for how he has tamed the rather messy world of R programming into a well-designed tidyverse . He is another thoughtful voice to listen to as we move into the world of agentic engineering , in this case by trying to figure out what the real cost of tokens is . I hear a lot of suspicion that AI tokens are unsustainably priced and that frontier labs are heavily subsidising costs with their VC money. They want to get us hooked now, so they can pull the rug out from under us whenever they want to make a bunch of money. Is that true? My sense is that it’s mostly not. But can I back that up with some data? His conclusion is that it doesn’t seem that token costs are significantly subsidized on per-token API basis, but they are with subscription plans. (He caveats his analysis, saying it doesn’t take into account recouping the costs of training the models.) ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ There’s a creepy excitement at the thought that models are clever enough to edit the weights of models, an activity that Takehi et al refer to as Weight-Space Programming . Just by looking at the raw weights, GPT-6 Astra can tell what a network was trained to do. And without any environment feedback, it has no trouble writing, from scratch, small game-playing networks that outplay networks trained with PPO for 100 million steps. While we don’t know if we’ll ever be able to download skills directly into our brains ( “I know kung fu” - or for those in my particular demographic: Joe 90 ), this does raise the possibility of downloading capabilities into models by manipulating their weights. Simon Wilison riffed on this paper by examining whether an LLM can understand model behaviors from the weights alone , by examining four simple neural networks, each trained to play a specific game, and figuring out which game it was by just looking at the weights. ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ Jessica Kerr (jessitron): My days of teaching AI to do stuff are numbered. Getting it to teach me stuff is more fun. ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ Houck et al (that “al” includes some folks who I’ve learned to pay a lot of attention to), look at how we can assess the quality of context supplied to agents. An agent may draw from source code, specifications, issue trackers, chat histories, architectural documents, tool output, and user instructions, then act on that combination with limited human supervision. Information that was written for different audiences, at different times, and for different purposes is brought together into a temporary operating environment for a particular task. Whether each source is individually useful does not reveal whether the resulting context is fit for the work the agent is being asked to do. They’ve come up with a framework for describing the quality of this assembled context , which they refer to as CAFE(S). The acronym refers to five dimensions they look at: Clarity: Can the agent interpret the request as intended? Actionability: Can the agent proceed, and know when it is done? Fidelity: Can the agent trust that this context is true? Efficiency: Can the agent focus on what matters? Security: Should the agent have this context at all? They also list a set of half-a-dozen “context smells”: common cases where these break down (and a nod to Kent’s original metaphor ) I’m not sure about the name, (how exactly should I pronounce “CAFE(S)”?) and the article exhibits rather more LLM Voice that I prefer. But on the whole I think this is a good framing for thinking about an important part of feeding our silicon servants/overlords. ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ Cindy Sridharan noted that the problems she ran into six months ago are no longer around : What was missing in my setup 6 months ago was the verification process I now use. 70% of my daily token spend goes into verifying patches, and only ~20-30% into creating them. That resonated with conversations I’ve had with folks using agents in enterprise settings. They are using far more tokens to check the working of models (through guardrails and evals) than they are to generate a response to a request. A single request to a model from a customer may trigger a dozen turns to other models to probe its input and verify its output.

piezas.titulo: GLM-5.4: Toward Generalized Coding with Our First Loop Transformer
piezas.resumenOriginal: GLM-5.4: Toward Generalized Coding with Our First Loop Transformer GLM 5.4 is now available from Chinese AI lab Z.ai. It's their first model to use a looped transformer architecture, which they describe like this: In a standard Transformer, each layer runs once per forward pass. In a Loop Transformer, a group of weight-shared layers runs for multiple iterations, refining the hidden states from the previous pass. This gives us a deeper network without increasing the parameter count. This is the second mention of looped transformers I've seen in the past week - the first was Inkling 2 Mini from Thinking Machines Lab on November 20th, who said: Inkling 2 Mini is a looped transformer, running the middle layers of the model three times for every token. This allows the model to apply more reasoning and reach the right answer with fewer tokens, especially on tasks such as agentic coding that depend on reasoning quality. GLM 5.4 is not yet available as open weights: We plan to open-source the model weights responsibly after completing necessary safety hardening. I tried it out using the Z.ai API, for which I had to sign up for their Coding Plan subscription because 5.4 cannot currently be accessed through the regular API. It turns out both coding plan and regular API share the same OpenAI-compatible Responses API (at https://api.z.ai/api/v1 ), and the API key for the coding plan worked with that and gave me access to the new model. I built a llm-glm plugin , then realized that llm-zai by Tommy Hughes already exists! I've shipped mine purely because llm-zai doesn't yet support the new model, but I'll likely retire mine once that plugin catches up. Here are pelicans for GLM-5.4 on low, high, and max. This is the max one: I realized I never ran pelicans for GLM-5.3, so here those are for the same effort levels. They look similar in quality to 5.4. It's interesting how GLM 5.1 and GLM 5.2 produced radically different pelicans from other models. The pelicans for 5.3 and 5.4 are much more comparable to those I get from OpenAI or Anthropic models - the previous generations had their own distinctive look. I made a comparison grid showing the four generations of GLM pelicans all in one place. The style transition between 5.2 and 5.3 is pretty stark. piezas.titulo: AI Is Giving Optical Computing Another Shot
piezas.resumenOriginal: The idea of computing with light has been around for over 70 years, but until recently it’s remained largely in the realm of research. Over the past few years, though, optical computing has emerged as a fast-growing industry: Market valuation of companies in this sector now totals US $2.22 billion, up from $0.4 billion in 2022. One projection suggests that the market will continue to grow exponentially in the coming years. The reason for this sudden surge will surprise no one: AI. In particular, AI inference—the process of using AI models to respond to user queries—has driven much of the construction of huge, power-hungry data centers, and relatively energy-efficient optical systems are seen as a potential way forward. “Most of the interest in [photonics] is driven by the fact that AI inference has literally become limited by power, and in a rather striking manner,” says Peter McMahon , associate professor of applied and engineering physics at Cornell University, in Ithaca, N.Y., who has researched optical computing for over a decade. Optics, at least on paper, carries the promise of doing the same math as today’s GPUs at a drastically lower level of power. Switching from electronics to optics would be a pretty radical solution. Nevertheless, like mushrooms after a rainstorm, optical-computing startups are popping up in the United States, China, Germany, and Israel. And while competing against such GPU makers as Nvidia is an ambitious goal, the investment in optical computing has spurred development of complementary approaches, such as designing alternative AI algorithms, taking on scientific computing, and enhancing in-network computing. Optalysys, based in England, is inserting optical-computing elements into the networking path, where data centers already use light. The company’s basic on-chip optical element, shown in the inset, is a Fourier transform calculator. Optalysys “I think it would be good for the technology if many of these companies made a good run at it,” says Logan Wright , assistant professor of applied physics at Yale University, in New Haven, Conn., and a former postdoc in McMahon’s lab. “I think that the technology that will be developed through this would be really, really useful, and enable photonic systems that maybe don’t get on this wave of AI but would be capable of doing really quite special things.” Optics to inference’s rescue? Inference makes up the bulk of AI energy use. The industry is already spending billions of dollars designing advanced GPUs and other chips to run inference as efficiently as possible. At the heart of the inference computation is one operation, done countless times a second: matrix-vector multiplication. Back in 1978, optical-computing pioneer Joseph W. Goodman and his coworkers proposed a method for doing matrix-vector multiplication with light. The setup was relatively simple. Let’s say a vector of length N needs to be multiplied by a matrix of size N by N . N light-emitting diodes, all in a row, encode the elements of the vector into the intensity of light—the brighter the light from an individual diode, the greater the value that diode encodes. Then, a cylindrical lens spreads out the light vertically, essentially copying the vector N times. The light then passes through an attenuator of N by N pixels. At each pixel, the light is attenuated according to the corresponding value at that location in the matrix. Passing the light through the attenuator performs the multiplication. Finally, a cylindrical lens oriented perpendicular to the first lens re-collects the light from each row, summing it up. The final vector is measured by a row of detectors. VECTOR-MATRIX MULTIPLICATION The most computationally expensive part of common AI today is vector-matrix (or matrix-matrix) multiplication. For a vector of length N (here, N = 3), it takes N 2 (here, 9) multiplication steps and three accumulation steps—multiple additions at once. The argument for why optics might be advantageous over electronics goes something like this: Multiplying a matrix of size N by N by a vector of length N takes N 2 multiplication steps. In electronics, each multiplication takes some energy, so the total energy used scales as N 2 . In optics, however, the multiplication step is passive: As long as the matrix stays the same, passing light through the attenuator costs almost no energy. The only cost is encoding the vector into light and reading out the answer, but the vector is of length N , not N 2 . So the energy used will scale as N , not N 2 , as bigger vectors and matrices are multiplied. Since Goodman’s 1978 proposal, the quality of the available optical elements has improved dramatically. Indeed, in 2022, a team of researchers at Cornell led by McMahon demonstrated an optical neural network that consumed less than one photon of energy—approximately 2.5 x 10 -19 joules—per multiplication operation. In a standard computer, a single multiply operation can take between 10 -14 and 10 -12 joules, which suggests that optics could possibly reduce energy use by a factor of 100,000. But McMahon cautions against such extrapolation. First, the cost of encoding data into optics was not included in the calculation. Even if the scaling is favorable with light, in practice it’s not just the scaling that matters, it’s also the coefficients. Let’s say the energy cost of doing one multiplication with electronics is 1 picojoule, and the cost to encode one vector element with optics is 1,000 picojoules. The electronic approach still wins if the length N of the vector is fewer than 1,000 elements. McMahon says this example is not far off from reality: “One of the key questions is, How big do you have to make the system before you start winning? Lots of people have done this calculation for various kinds of neural networks. The very rough answer is somewhere between N equals 1,000 and N equals 10,000.” It’s also important to keep in mind a computing principle known as Amdahl’s law . “Amdahl’s law shouldn’t even be called a law. It’s a simple piece of common sense,” McMahon says. “If you have something that’s going to accelerate a computation, and it can accelerate 90 percent of the code, but there’s 10 percent of the code that it can’t accelerate, then the maximum possible speedup you can get is 10x.” With AI inferencing, the point is to save energy, not time. But Amdahl’s observation still applies. What fraction of today’s AI inferencing code can be better handled with optics is a complicated question that varies by approach. But it’s not 100 percent. Matrix-vector multiplication, or matrix-matrix multiplication, is only part of the inference workload—there are other, nonlinear operations that need to be performed on the data. Taking all of these caveats into account, optical-computing companies today are aiming for a 10- to 80-fold improvement in energy efficiency over today’s GPUs. The question is whether they can deliver on that promise at scale before traditional electronics catches up to those gains. Bridging the gap in free space The startup Lumai , based in Oxford, England, has taken perhaps the most direct inspiration from Goodman and his team. Lumai’s head of product, Phillip Burr , declares that a free-space approach, where the light travels through air rather than on-chip waveguides, is what will enable the company’s tech to beat GPUs. Instead of the fixed attenuator used in Goodman’s proposal, Lumai is using a modern programmable device called a spatial light modulator—a pixelated membrane akin to a fancy liquid-crystal display that can modulate both the intensity and phase of light. The rest of the design is more sophisticated in practice but similar in principle to Goodman’s design: A vector is encoded into light, copied N times via a lens, passed through the spatial light modulator, collected with another lens, and the result is converted back to digital electronics. The electronics then handle the nonlinear functions. “A full vector-matrix multiply completes in a single optical cycle,” Burr says. To accurately compare the energy expenditures of the optical and GPU approaches, you must first specify which part of the workload you’re considering. Modern inference is often split into two phases: prefill , where the input query is processed and propagated through the model, and decode , where the output is generated one word (or token) at a time. Prefill is the more computationally intensive of the two. It basically involves doing vector-matrix multiplications for the same matrix over and over. Decode also involves vector-matrix multiplies, but not as intensively—the time-consuming part of decode is reading the necessary matrices in and out of memory. Vector-matrix multiplication with free-space optics The Goodman optical computer is the simplest version of a photonic vector-matrix multiplier. Here, the vector elements are encoded into the intensity of light from three light sources, such as LEDs. Then, a cylindrical lens spreads the light vertically. The matrix elements are encoded into the opacity of an attenuator, such that when light passes through each pixel it is multiplied (attenuated) by that matrix value. Finally, another cylindrical lens collects the light horizontally, performing the accumulation step, and a photodetector measures the output vector. Lumai, and other companies in the space, are focusing on the compute-intensive prefill phase of inference. Lumai claims that its Iris Nova optical server, made available for evaluation in April 2026, is a proof of concept, and its next-generation Iris Aura server will do prefill using roughly one-tenth of the energy a GPU would use. The startup Neurophos , based in Austin, Texas, is putting a different spin on the Goodman computer design. To pack more punch into a small device, the company is leveraging its expertise in metamaterials—complex structures that can manipulate light at scales smaller than a single wavelength. The structures it has designed are bigger than a wavelength but still quite small—just several micrometers per side. “The equivalent of the optical transistor that you can get from standard silicon photonics today is like 2 millimeters long,” says Patrick Bowen , CEO of Neurophos. “You just can’t fit enough [of] them on-chip to get a compute density that remotely competes with the latest and greatest [that] TSMC [Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co.] does.” Bowen’s team designed metamaterial-based modulators that can be programmed to manipulate the phase and intensity of light at the micrometer scale, resulting in an array of 1,000 by 1,000 modulators in a square chip with 5-mm sides. According to Bowen, Neurophos’s modulators switch over 10,000 times as fast as a standard liquid-crystal spatial light modulators do. Bowen also claims a performance advantage over Nvidia’s Blackwell GPU: “We’re targeting 50 times Blackwell B200’s speed and 35 times its energy efficiency, and have a road map to reach 250 times the speed and roughly 90 times the energy efficiency in subsequent generations.” The approach is CMOS-compatible, Bowen says, which should allow Neurophos to manufacture its chips on the semiconductor industry’s existing high-volume production lines. The company is currently choosing a site for a production facility ahead of its rack deliveries to customers in 2028. Both Lumai and Neurophos are betting they’ll get their products to market before traditional CMOS can catch up to their energy savings. “Silicon will keep improving, but digital efficiency gains now come slowly and at rising cost,” Burr says. “Optics offers a different scaling relationship, in which efficiency improves as matrices grow. Larger models, longer context windows, and agentic workloads are all pushing prefill in that direction.” Bridging the gap on-chip Free-space optics carries the promise of almost energy-free multiplication, as in Goodman’s design. But another big advance in optics since Goodman’s work in the 1970s is integrated photonics, which allows you to guide and manipulate light on-chip. “The name of the game is to do as large a vector size as possible to maximize the benefit of using optics, and for that reason the free-space approaches are promising,” says Yale’s Logan Wright. “But it’s still fundamentally harder” to use the free-space approach, “because there’s just so much less infrastructure than in silicon photonics.” Other companies—like Shanghai-based Lightelligence and Q.ANT , based in Stuttgart, Germany—are trading the 3D advantage of free-space optics for the manufacturability of photonics integrated directly onto a silicon chip. “There is a good reason that free-space optics are usually limited to 1,000 units a year,” says Q.ANT’s CEO and founder, Michael Förtsch . “The reason for this is lens inspection, assembly strategy, and so on. Semiconductor-manufacturable integrated photonic circuits are at this point way more promising to reach volume production.” Vector-matrix multiplication with integrated photonics One way to do vector-matrix multiplication with light on-chip involves encoding vector elements into the amplitudes of pulses of light, traveling sequentially through a waveguide. The multiplication is performed by Mach-Zehnder interferometers: A waveguide splits in two, and the phase of light traveling through one of the paths is shifted by a controlled voltage. When the two paths reunite, the resulting light intensity depends on that phase shift, performing a multiplication. Encoding the matrix elements into the phase shifts turns this into vector-matrix multiplication. A photodetector then collects the light from all three pulses, performing the accumulation step. In Q.ANT’s approach, the input data is encoded into the phase and amplitude of light pulses via on-chip modulators. A vector in this scheme is represented as a sequence of such pulses, each representing one vector element. The light is guided around the chip with waveguides. The basic computational element is an interferometer: A waveguide splits into two paths, and the light beam traveling down one path is subjected to a phase shift, controlled by a set voltage. When the two paths recombine, the resulting interference performs a computation. Then, photodetectors and analog-to-digital converters turn the result back into digital data. The serialized vector-matrix multiplication approach is slower than Goodman’s computer, where the whole calculation happens at once. However, the slower speed can be mitigated by using multiple wavelengths at once, effectively encoding multiple vectors into light simultaneously. Q.ANT’s Native Processing Server is already being used in research institutions like the Leibniz Supercomputing Centre in Munich and the Jülich Supercomputing Centre in Jülich, both in Germany. Earlier this year, the company announced a commercial sale to the cloud provider Ionos. Similarly, Lightelligence’s PACE2 processor is capable of multiplying 128-by-128-element matrices. In a paper released in 2025, the company described vector-matrix multiplication at a 1-gigahertz frequency and 3-nanosecond latency, claiming two orders of magnitude lower latency than with traditional GPUs. The energy advantage is yet to be conclusively demonstrated, however, and Q.ANT’s Förtsch admits there is still a ways to go. The main issue is the energy cost of analog-to-digital conversion and back. As long as a fast, low-energy converter does not exist, Förtsch says, “we don’t see realistic chances that…a general vector-matrix multiplication machine in optics makes sense.” Beyond matrix-vector multiplication Not everyone in the field is focused on matrix-vector multiplication, despite it being all the rage in the AI inference world. In fact, while the optical vector-matrix multiply idea goes back to the 1970s, other computations with optics have been investigated as far back as the 1950s. For example, a Fourier transform—a common operation that decomposes a complex wave or signal into its constituent frequencies—can be done in optics with a single lens. “A digital chip has to approximate [Fourier transforms] in many small steps, using hundreds to thousands of transistors and more compute cycles,” says Q.ANT’s Förtsch. “Models that use such nonlinear functions can reach the same or better accuracy with fewer parameters and fewer operations.” Even though Q.ANT’s optical processor has been used for traditional vector-matrix multiplication, the company believes its greatest advantages lie in alternative AI architectures that leverage more complex functions. “Tasks such as image classification and segmentation rely heavily on operations like Fourier series, transformations, and other nonlinear functions, which photonics handles natively. We see similar potential in generative AI, especially image and video generation,” Förtsch says. The Israel-based startup LightSolver is also targeting algorithms that are a more natural fit for its device. “If you look at propagating electromagnetic waves, essentially, they are running differential equations in their nature,” says Ruti Ben-Shlomi , CEO and cofounder of LightSolver. She says differential equations can be solved much faster and with higher energy efficiency on the company’s laser processing unit (LPU) than on a traditional computer. LightSolver’s LPU is an interesting twist on the Goodman optical-computer design. It has input light, a programmable membrane in the form of a spatial light modulator, and output light, but the whole thing is placed in a cavity, where light bounces back and forth many times before reaching a steady state. In addition, the team places a gain medium inside the cavity. This gain medium functions much like those found inside a laser, causing the bouncing light to build up in intensity. LightSolver, a startup based in Israel, is using free-space optics to quickly solve differential equations by harnessing the natural properties of light. LightSolver Once a particular problem is encoded into the modulator, the gain medium is stimulated to emit random photons. They bounce back and forth, increasing in intensity when passing through the gain medium again, experiencing preprogrammed changes through the modulator and interacting with one another until they reach a steady state—the solution. Then, a simple camera takes a picture of the steady-state result. Using emulation, the LightSolver team recently showed that their LPU can solve differential equations 40 to 80,000 times as fast as a GPU, depending on the workflow. They are now working on explicitly benchmarking the energy improvements. LightSolver’s team is currently working on AI applications for its LPU as well, using the company’s own algorithm to do image generation from text. “We’re not doing vector-matrix multiplication very fast. We are doing something different. We need to assume that the way you train the model, and you then do inference, is completely different. But if you do it differently, you’ll be able to do image generation with dramatic energy-consumption decrease and speedup,” Ben-Shlomi says. LightSolver has a working prototype of its LPU, and the team is working on a larger, rack-mountable box. Computing in transit Yet another way to leverage light’s particular strengths is being pursued by Optalysys , a startup based in Leeds, England. Nick New , founder and chief product officer, has a background in free-space optics, and so he understood that taking a Fourier transform is very easy to do with light. The key idea behind Optalysys’s technology is taking that Fourier capability of optics in free space and making it work on-chip. “Rather than using a lens these days, we have our own component, which is a passive component in the plane of the silicon that does that same job,” New says. And by cleverly designing that component with multiple outputs, the team figured out how to perform different operations as well. “Because of how the Fourier transform response is generated, you can actually pull out different mathematical operations from it,” New says. “We can produce very large, high-precision digital functions at superhigh efficiencies, using our analog photonics approach.” “We’re effectively adding processing to where there is none right now.” —Nick New, Optalysis Instead of redesigning an accelerator from scratch, Optalysys is targeting a piece of the AI workload that’s often already in the optical domain: networking. In the data center, racks of computers are connected to each other with fiber optics, and the optical connections are increasingly getting closer and closer to the GPUs and CPUs themselves. Some computations already happen while the data is en route. These computations, which include combining results from multiple GPUs, are executed inside network switch cards. But the cards naturally use power to do that math. With passive optical components, these computations could be done essentially for free. New says that in addition to communication between GPUs, Optalysys’s technology could be used to facilitate a GPU’s communication with memory, doing things like compression and format conversion on the fly. Going back to AI inference, this approach could improve the decode part of the workload. Unlike prefill, decode is memory bound: The most costly part is shuffling model data in and out of memory. “We’re more focused on the memory-bound applications, which fits very well with this principle of adding processing into the communication path,” New says. “We’re effectively adding processing to where there is none right now.” The likely future of optical computing How likely are optical computers to replace GPUs in the data center? Yale’s Wright is not too optimistic. “The direction of algorithm development is not going to be a direction that is automatically favorable for optics,” he says. “In fact, it’s most likely to go in the opposite direction, because [AI model developers] want it to work better on GPUs.” However, even if our AI queries aren’t going to be computed in light in the next few years, that investment in the technology won’t be in vain. Says Wright, “The reason that I and many other people in the field are at least somewhat optimistic is that there’s real investment from companies like Nvidia and TSMC in developing co-packaged silicon photonics—not for computing, but for circuit switching and interconnects, and that just kind of opens the door to do a little bit more in the future.” Whether that technology ends up crunching vector-matrix multiplication, doing bespoke simulations, or performing in-network computations, the computing ecosystem seems ripe for a variety of approaches. “We see the data center of the future as heterogeneous: CPUs, GPUs and photonic NPUs [native processing units] each take on the tasks they are best suited for,” says Q.ANT’s Förtsch. “Running each task on the most efficient hardware can significantly reduce energy use and operating costs.” This article appears in the December 2026 print issue as “The Return of the Optical Computer.”

piezas.titulo: Comparative effectiveness, clinical importance, and certainty of acupuncture-based therapies for post-stroke depression: a systematic review and network meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
piezas.resumenOriginal: ObjectiveTo compare the relative effectiveness of acupuncture and acupuncture-based combination therapies for post-stroke depression (PSD) and to assess the certainty of evidence for the key outcomes.MethodsSix databases were searched from inception to March 1, 2026. Random-effects network meta-analyses compared eight treatment strategies for depressive symptoms, neurological impairment, and activities of daily living. HAMD results were synthesized as standardized mean differences (SMDs) to accommodate different scale versions; SDS, NIHSS, and MBI results were expressed as mean differences. Clinical interpretation considered confidence intervals, outcome-specific reference benchmarks where applicable, and CINeMA certainty ratings. A common three-point HAMD threshold was not applied across versions.ResultsWe included 125 randomized controlled trials involving 10,251 participants. ACU-rTMS had the highest HAMD ranking and was associated with lower scores than antidepressants (SMD, −2.17; 95% CI, −3.63 to −0.70) and standard care (SMD, −3.30; 95% CI, −4.86 to −1.74), with moderate-certainty evidence. Its comparison with rTMS remained uncertain (SMD, −1.17; 95% CI, −2.35 to 0.01; low certainty). A validated common HAMD threshold for clinical importance was unavailable. SDS and functional outcomes suggested potential benefits, but confidence intervals frequently included effects below the reference benchmarks. Of 86 network comparisons, none had high-certainty evidence. Comparative safety could not be established.ConclusionAcupuncture-based therapies may improve selected outcomes in PSD. ACU-rTMS is promising, but its incremental benefit over rTMS and the clinical importance of its standardized HAMD effects remain uncertain. Heterogeneity, possible measurement and small-study biases, predominantly middle-aged and older Chinese populations, and limited safety and long-term data restrict clinical recommendations.Systematic review registrationhttps://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420261465363.

piezas.titulo: A neuro-computational framework for modeling developmental changes in cross-sensory interactions in autism
piezas.resumenOriginal: Recent studies have shown that multisensory processing in children shifts from a competitive to a facilitative state as development progresses, and this transition appears delayed in children with autism spectrum diagnosis (ASD). The neural mechanisms underlying this developmental change, and its alteration in ASD, remain largely unknown. To address this gap, we investigated how sensory modalities interact in the developing brain using a biologically plausible neuro-computational model governed by Hebbian learning rules. We also explored the neural substrates that may underlie atypical multisensory development in ASD. Our results suggest that the net effective influence of cross-modal interactions gradually shifts from suppressive to facilitatory during development, mediating the observed shift from competition to facilitation in typical children. Furthermore, our simulations show that the delayed transition in ASD may stem either from reduced neural plasticity or diminished multisensory experience. Our model provides a computational framework for examining how differences in multisensory experience and in the rate of synaptic weight updating may shape the developmental trajectory of cross-modal interactions. By linking computational modeling with behavioral findings, our work provides a framework for understanding atypical sensory development.

destilado.texto: El paso de interacción sensorial competitiva a facilitadora se retrasa en niños con diagnóstico de autismo. El alcance potencial de estas peticiones quedaba restringido a la consulta de información auxiliar y a determinados estados de configuración. piezas.titulo: Frequency-specific cortical swallowing-network responses following neuroengineering-guided individualized multichannel tDCS.
piezas.resumenOriginal: Background Neuromodulatory interventions for dysphagia are increasingly explored as adjunctive rehabilitation strategies, yet their efficacy may be limited by non-individualized stimulation protocols and insufficient consideration of network-specific brain dynamics. Advances in neuroengineering now enable individualized targeting based on functional neuroimaging and computational modeling, offering the potential for precision neuromodulation of swallowing-related brain networks. Methods We investigated whether individualized multichannel transcranial direct current stimulation (mc-tDCS), optimized using magnetoencephalography (MEG)-derived target localization, MRI-based finite-element head modeling, and a distributed constrained maximum intensity (D-CMI) optimization framework, modulates the cortical swallowing network. In a randomized sham-controlled crossover design, eight healthy adults underwent three stimulation conditions: low-intensity mc-tDCS (1.5 mA), high-intensity mc-tDCS (4.0 mA), and sham stimulation. Swallowing-related cortical activity was assessed before and after stimulation using MEG source reconstruction of event-related desynchronization during uncued voluntary swallowing and a visually cued swallowing task requiring precise timing. A repeated-measures Dose × Task × Time model tested the hypothesized interaction separately in five frequency bands, with Holm correction across bands. Results No Dose × Task × Time interaction was significant after Holm correction across the five frequency bands (all adjusted p ≥ 0.274). Within-condition pre-post analyses identified alpha- and beta-band changes after 1.5-mA stimulation during challenged swallowing and a low-gamma change after 4.0-mA stimulation during uncued swallowing. Challenged-task timing accuracy increased over time, without significant Dose or Dose × Time effects. Conclusions This study demonstrates the feasibility of integrating individualized MEG-based targeting, subject-specific head modeling, and optimized multichannel stimulation. The hypothesized Dose × Task × Time interaction was not significant. Exploratory within-condition pre-post differences were observed in alpha, beta, and low-gamma activity, but do not establish stimulation-specific effects. Larger controlled studies are needed to evaluate the physiological effects of this individualized approach.

piezas.titulo: A Practical Guide to Understanding Interoception and Translating Knowledge into Practice.
piezas.resumenOriginal: Growing recognition of the relationship between interoception, self-regulation, and occupational participation has increased clinical interest in interoception within pediatric occupational therapy. However, translating interoception science into practice remains challenging because interoception is multidimensional, current assessments cannot precisely identify the processes contributing to a child's occupational difficulties, and evidence supporting available interventions remains limited. In this paper, we present an overview of the neuroscience of interoception and offer the Interoception Ladder Framework, a conceptual clinical reasoning tool for planning and evaluating interoception-informed occupational therapy. We position comprehensive assessment and collaborative, participation-focused goal setting as guides for intervention planning, with co-regulation and caregiver coaching embedded throughout. We propose three inter-related intervention rungs addressing mind-body awareness, arousal regulation, and explicit interoceptive awareness training. Intervention selection and sequencing are individualized and iterative. We suggest a planned review point at which therapists can examine whether occupational performance has improved. When participation is not improving, we encourage therapists to review their clinical reasoning, reconsider the intervention target, and assess whether activities, environments or contextual demands need to be modified. We position occupational participation as the primary outcome of interoception-informed occupational therapy, placing change in interoceptive awareness as secondary. Empirical evaluation is required to establish the framework's validity, feasibility, and clinical utility.

piezas.titulo: Developmental timing of gene expression predicts dosage dominance, which tracks neuronal-glial fate in the developing human brain
piezas.resumenOriginal: Genes implicated in brain disorders have diverse functions, but how altered dosage shapes their effects on developmental cell fate remains unclear. In a cell-state dynamics model of the developing human brain, genes expressed earlier in development responded more strongly to knockout than to overexpression, and this dosage dominance tracked neuronal-glial fate. Fate responses of 14,044 genes formed 31 modules across 21 lineages. Stronger perturbations could reverse fate responses despite correlated predicted expression changes across neuronal destinations. Disease-risk genes occupied shared and distinct developmental programs. Within autism, module timing distinguished genes associated with and without intellectual disability or developmental delay, while de novo and common variation implicated different modules. Knockout signatures of selected autism-associated modules matched the neuronal-down, glial-up pattern that postmortem autism cortex shares with other psychiatric disorders. These findings connect heterogeneous genetic risk through developmental programs whose fate responses depend on dosage and cellular context.

Mientras que el PLN resulta eficaz a la hora de identificar patrones lingüísticos, la psicología articula la investigación definiendo los conceptos clave, explicando su relevancia y aportando un marco para interpretar los hallazgos. La ponencia comienza con varios estudios de caso centrados en la supervivencia al cáncer, la identificación de problemas de salud mental en la población general y la exploración de momentos de felicidad en personas diagnosticadas con depresión, todos ellos a partir de datos en inglés. A continuación, aborda consideraciones transculturales al trabajar con datos en idiomas distintos del inglés y evalúa los modelos del lenguaje de gran tamaño (LLM) para este fin. La presentación subraya que un PLN fundamentado en la teoría puede desvelar trayectorias psicológicas y ofrecer perspectivas valiosas para las intervenciones terapéuticas. No obstante, también destaca cómo la falta de datos de calidad y de evaluaciones adecuadas plantea retos a la hora de desarrollar métodos aplicables a lenguas más allá del inglés. Reseña: Ana-Maria Bucur es investigadora postdoctoral en el Instituto Dalle Molle de Inteligencia Artificial (IDSIA), Università della Svizzera italiana, donde trabaja en el Laboratorio de Recuperación de Información del profesor Fabio Crestani. Realizó un doctorado en cotutela entre la Universitat Politècnica de València y la Universidad de Bucarest, bajo la dirección de los profesores Paolo Rosso y Liviu P. Dinu. Ana-Maria ha participado en colaboraciones interdisciplinares que abarcan tanto la psicología como las humanidades digitales. Su investigación se centra principalmente en el procesamiento del lenguaje natural (PLN) aplicado a la salud mental, investigando en especial cómo las personas expresan sus estados psicológicos a través del lenguaje y de qué manera los métodos computacionales pueden mejorar nuestra comprensión de la salud mental y respaldar el bienestar. Más recientemente, ha estado explorando cómo influye la cultura en las manifestaciones de los trastornos mentales y cómo desarrollar métodos computacionales con sensibilidad cultural para un cribado de salud mental más inclusivo. piezas.titulo: Task-specific sensorimotor rhythm dynamics during action observation in chronic stroke and healthy adults
piezas.resumenOriginal: Action Observation Therapy (AOT) is used in rehabilitation research because observing goal-directed actions may engage neural processes relevant to motor learning after stroke. However, the neurophysiological responses elicited by different types of observed actions, and their temporal evolution, remain incompletely understood. Previous EEG work showed that goal-directed activities of daily living, particularly the reaching phases of feeding and self-care actions, elicit stronger sensorimotor rhythm suppression in chronic stroke survivors. We therefore investigated task-specific rhythm modulation during observation of activities of daily living in healthy participants and individuals with chronic stroke. Twenty stroke survivors with right hemiparesis (≥6 months post-stroke) and 23 healthy controls were included. Participants observed standardized videos of finalized and non-finalized actions, as well as control videos. EEG Event-Related Spectral Perturbation analysis was used to assess power changes in the α-(8–13 Hz) and β-band (14–25 Hz) bands across temporal intervals and action categories. Linear mixed-effects models examined within- and between-group effects. Both groups exhibited greater reactivity at central scalp sites during finalized actions than during control videos. Healthy participants showed earlier and more pronounced β-band desynchronization. Individuals with stroke showed delayed and weaker β-band suppression, particularly over the affected hemisphere, while retaining responses to goal-directed actions. The main between-group β-band differences persisted after adjustment for age. During feeding actions, stroke participants showed a lower β-desynchronization peak frequency at C3 than healthy controls (15.3 vs. 17.5 Hz), remaining significant after age adjustment (p = 0.003) and correction for multiple comparisons. Self-care and feeding actions were associated with more sustained modulation, whereas external and non-finalized actions showed earlier rebound patterns, particularly in healthy participants. These findings indicate that goal-directed activities of daily living are associated with distinct temporal patterns of baseline-referenced oscillatory activity and support further evaluation of task-specific stimuli in future AOT studies. The EEG findings should not be interpreted as direct or specific evidence of mirror-neuron-system activation or as evidence of treatment efficacy.

destilado.texto: Observar acciones cotidianas activa más la desincronización del ritmo sensorimotor que ver videos neutros. piezas.titulo: Efficacy of high-frequency versus low-frequency repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation for post-stroke upper limb motor dysfunction: a meta-analysis
piezas.resumenOriginal: BackgroundBoth high-frequency and low-frequency repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) can improve upper limb motor function after stroke; however, the difference in efficacy between the two modalities and the impact of disease stage on treatment efficacy remain unclear.ObjectiveTo systematically compare the efficacy of high-frequency versus low-frequency rTMS for post-stroke upper limb motor dysfunction, and to explore the influence of disease stage on efficacy through subgroup analysis.MethodsA systematic search of Embase, PubMed, Cochrane Library, Web of Science, and CNKI was conducted to identify randomized controlled trials comparing high-frequency or low-frequency rTMS with sham stimulation or conventional rehabilitation, and head-to-head comparisons of high-frequency versus low-frequency rTMS. Meta-analysis was performed using RevMan 5.4, and subgroup analysis was conducted according to disease stage.ResultsA total of 23 RCTs were included. The direct comparison between high-frequency and low-frequency rTMS showed no significant difference in overall efficacy (MD = 0.89, 95% CI: −0.42 to 2.20, p = 0.18). In the acute-stage subgroup, high-frequency rTMS showed a statistically significant but clinically modest difference (MD = 2.76, 95% CI 0.74–4.77, p = 0.007); however, the test for subgroup differences was not statistically significant (p = 0.05), so this within-subgroup finding does not establish a stage-specific effect. No significant difference was observed in the subacute or chronic stages. The control comparisons were directionally similar, but they are indirect and provide descriptive context only.ConclusionHigh-frequency and low-frequency rTMS have comparable overall efficacy for post-stroke upper limb motor function. Within the acute-stage subgroup, high-frequency rTMS was associated with greater FMA-UE improvement; however, the between-stage difference was not statistically significant (p = 0.05), the pooled estimate did not reach the MCID threshold, and the certainty of evidence was low. This finding should therefore be regarded as exploratory and hypothesis-generating.

piezas.titulo: Cortical thinning and functional reorganization as well as related transcriptomic signatures during early motor recovery following acute basal ganglia ischemic stroke.
piezas.resumenOriginal: Background Acute basal ganglia ischemic stroke (ABGIS) commonly causes severe motor impairment, yet early spatiotemporal patterns of cortical morphological alterations and functional reorganization alongside the spatially coupled transcriptomic signatures remain unclear. Methods Twenty-six ABGIS patients and thirty-three normal controls (NCs) received multimodal MRI and neurological examinations, and patients were reassessed at 1-month follow-up. Cortical morphological changes and brain functional reorganization were analyzed based on cortical thickness (CT) and functional connectivity (FC). We identified the most discriminative FC features based on machine learning (ML) classification and interpretability analyses, and investigated transcriptomic signatures associated with FC alterations via the Allen Human Brain Atlas. Results No differences in CT were found between baseline ABGIS patients (ABGIS_1) and NCs. Compared with ABGIS_1, follow-up patients (ABGIS_2) exhibited reduced CT in the left postcentral gyrus (PoCG.L), left superior parietal lobule (SPL.L), and left supramarginal gyrus (SMG.L). Compared with NCs, ABGIS_1 showed decreased FC from PoCG.L/SPL.L to sensorimotor cortex and occipital cortex. ABGIS_2 presented elevated FC relative to ABGIS_1 between PoCG.L and the right precentral gyrus (PreCG.R), and between SPL.L and the bilateral precentral gyrus as well as right superior occipital gyrus. Longitudinal increases in FC between PoCG.L/SPL.L and PreCG.R were positively correlated with improvements in Fugl-Meyer Assessment scores. ML models coupled with interpretability analyses preliminarily demonstrated that FC between PoCG.L/SPL.L and PreCG.R made prominent contributions to classification. Transcriptomic analysis revealed that gene sets correlated with FC alterations were mainly enriched in neuronal synaptic structure and synaptic signaling, chromatin regulation, as well as DNA and RNA metabolism. Conclusions This study verifies progressive cortical thinning and adaptive functional reorganization during early motor recovery following ABGIS, with such brain functional alterations paralleling distinct transcriptomic signatures, providing neuropathological and spatial transcriptomic clues for interpreting early motor recovery.

piezas.titulo: Kolpona: An Agentic Framework with Gradient-Free Neuron Programming for RTL Generation
piezas.resumenOriginal: arXiv:2611.33973v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Open-weight large language models (LLMs) for register-transfer level (RTL) design are usually improved by fine-tuning on curated Verilog corpora, which needs large sets of verified designs and GPU training. We present Kolpona, an agentic framework that improves such models without gradient training. Its first component is neuron programming, a new form of weight-space programming (WSP) that writes single neurons in closed form into the weights to remove failure habits found on practice tasks, and keeps each edit only when testbench results on fresh tasks favour it. At inference time, tool-using agents propose designs, and a label-free selection stage delivers one design per task from the specification, the candidates and their simulations alone. On Qwen3.5-4B, edits to 16 neurons raise the VerilogEval v2 pass@1 of the model alone from 31.7% to 55.4%, and the full framework reaches 77.6%. On Qwen3.8-27B, Kolpona lifts pass@1 from 73.1% to 94.9% on VerilogEval v2 and from 66.0% to 92.0% on RTLLM v2.1 on a single 32 GB GPU, above every published system in our comparison. The RTL edits also carry over to Python and raise the pass@1 of the 4B model alone from 84.8% to 91.5% on HumanEval+ and from 67.7% to 77.5% on MBPP+.

piezas.titulo: Effectiveness of Drive-Fun Intervention: Randomized Controlled Trial to Reduce Driving Risks Among Adolescents With ADHD.
piezas.resumenOriginal: ImportanceAdolescents with Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) are more likely to be involved in motor vehicle accidents, highlighting the need for early intervention. However, there is a lack of evidence-based interventions addressing driving safety in this population.ObjectiveTo evaluate the effectiveness of the Drive-Fun cognitive-functional intervention on simulated driving performance, attentional control, and visual scanning in adolescents with ADHD.DesignRandomized controlled trial with three parallel groups: Drive-Fun, an educational intervention, and a control group.SettingA university research laboratory.ParticipantsNinety-three adolescents ( M age = 16.8 years, SD = 0.52) diagnosed with ADHD.Outcomes and MeasuresPrimary outcomes were simulated driving errors; secondary outcomes included the percentage of time spent within the optimal Cognitive Effort Index (CEI) range and eye-tracking metrics.ResultsThe Drive-Fun group demonstrated significant time-by-group interactions: reduced driving errors, F (2, 89) = 82.65, p F (2, 89) = 15.56, p F (2, 89) = 27.65, p F (2, 89) = 7.61, p = .001, and pedestrians, F (2, 89) = 10.15, p < .001. Exploratory moderation analyses indicated greater improvements in driving performance among adolescents with lower Conners Hyperactive Scores and no regular sports participation within the Drive-Fun group.Conclusions and RelevanceThe Drive-Fun intervention improved simulated driving performance, cognitive engagement, and visual scanning, indicating its potential to reduce driving-related risks among adolescents with ADHD. Improvements were maintained at follow up, indicating sustained benefits. These findings support integrating cognitive-functional strategies and simulation-based training into occupational therapy to enhance adolescents' driving readiness and safety.

piezas.titulo: Two Nonprofits Join Forces to Support Adolescents on Autism Spectrum
piezas.resumenOriginal: Two Nonprofits Join Forces to Support Adolescents on Autism Spectrum STAR Admin Thu, 06/15/2017 - 14:07 STAR Institute for Sensory Processing Disorder (SPD) and T.A.C.T. (Teaching the Autism Community Trades) are two Colorado nonprofits who have partnered to create a series of respite camps serving adolescents who have autism spectrum disorder (ASD). Developmental Pathways has awarded the organizations a $25,000 grant to fund three F.U.S.E. (Fostering Unlimited Success and Empowerment) camps through 2018. STAR Institute offers premier treatment for SPD and brings expertise in social skills while T.AC.T. teaches trade and life skills to individuals with ASD and SPD with an emphasis on fostering independence and personal growth. “This is a very rare and exciting way to see two nonprofits interact. Our partnership to create F.U.S.E. allows both of our organizations to combine expertise in a way that best serves these adolescents to find new interests and gain the soft skills to successfully participate in peer groups and future workplaces”, says Dick Layton, Director of STAR Institute for SPD. The respite camps will be week-long day camps that host six students per camp ages 12-15 who have autism spectrum disorder. The camps will teach pre-vocational and vocational skills in a supportive, social, and inclusionary environment. Each camp has a different project for participants including: building a non-motorized go-cart with a partner, building an instrument to play in a band, and crafting board games. “The intended focus of F.U.S.E. is not just about offering a respite program for families. By generating new experiences for these adolescents, we hope to foster new skills, new interests, develop social skills, and give them a sense of empowerment to participate in what hopefully becomes a new hobby or future career interest”, says Danny Combs co-founder and president of T.A.C.T. SPD is a neurological disorder that disrupts the way an individual processes and responds to sensations. The disorder can affect people in only one sense–for example, just touch or just sight or just movement–or in multiple senses. One person with SPD may over-respond to touch sensation and find clothing, physical contact, other tactile sensory input to be unbearable and/or they may respond to visual or auditory or another sensory input. Another person might under-respond and show little or no reaction to stimulation, even pain or extreme hot and cold or just may be slow to respond to sensation. SPD and ASD have a high co-morbidity rate, but are also found to be standalone disorders. ASD refers to conditions categorized by challenges with social skills, repetitive behaviors, speech and nonverbal communication, as well as by unique strengths and differences that can occur on a range from mild to severe. Individuals with ASD and SPD frequently struggle with interpersonal skills over their lifetime and are often underestimated, which can lead to specific difficulty in career and relationships. F.U.S.E. aims to give individuals the ability to ignite new interests and feel empowered in group collaboration, which can lead to greater success in career and relationships. About STAR Institute for Sensory Processing Disorder: The STAR Institute for Sensory Processing Disorder, a Colorado 501(c)(3), is the world leader in treatment, research, and education for Sensory Processing Disorder, a neurological condition that disrupts the daily lives of more than 4 million Americans. The STAR Institute is the premier treatment center for children, adults and families living with Sensory Processing Disorder, feeding disorders, and other sensory conditions associated with ADHD, autism, and other developmental disorders. Dr. Lucy Jane Miller, founder of STAR Institute, is widely recognized as the leader in Sensory Processing Disorder research worldwide. For more information about the Greenwood Village, Colorado clinic, visit http://www.spdSTAR.org or call 303-221-7827. About T.A.C.T.
