Early vocational training helps young adults before they leave high school and sets them up for long term success. Our programs are designed to empower individuals and develop interests and skills for life. To learn more visit: https://tactkids.org or call 720-460-0897. About Developmental Pathways: Developmental Pathways is a 501(c)(3) nonprofit agency serving individuals with developmental disabilities/delays and their families. We are also one of Colorado’s Community Centered Boards (CCB) connecting people to federal, state, county, and private funding in Arapahoe County, Douglas County, and the City of Aurora. We passionately believe inclusion is for everyone and offer services through Home and Community Based Medicaid Waiver programs, locally funded programs, and partnerships with other community organizations. piezas.titulo: Therapist-supported versus self-guided digital CBT for chronic pain with neurodevelopmental traits: A pilot feasibility randomized controlled trial.
piezas.resumenOriginal: Background Chronic pain frequently co-occurs with neurodevelopmental disorders (NDDs) such as autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). If these traits are overlooked, standard cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) may be less effective. We developed a brief digital CBT program that adds psychoeducation on NDD traits to standard CBT for chronic pain. This study primarily examined its feasibility in adults with chronic pain and comorbid NDDs. Methods In this three-arm pilot feasibility randomized controlled trial, 44 adults with chronic pain and a self-reported diagnosis of ASD or ADHD were randomized to therapist-supported digital CBT (n = 15), self-guided digital CBT (n = 16), or a sham condition (n = 13; daily submission of the weekday and weather). The program comprised ten 15-min videos over two weeks. Primary outcomes were feasibility and pain catastrophizing; depressive symptoms were exploratory. Mixed models for repeated measures were used. Results Post-intervention retention was 90.9% (40/44). Of 31 participants allocated to CBT, 29 (93.5%) completed the program, all rating it as safe. Compared with sham, pain catastrophizing decreased significantly more in both the self-guided and therapist-supported groups ( p = .006 and p = .035), with no clear difference between the two CBT formats. Depressive symptoms showed a similar pattern. Other outcomes did not differ. Conclusions A brief digital CBT program for this population appears feasible and acceptable. Preliminary estimates favored both CBT formats but were imprecise because the trial was not powered for between-group comparisons. An adequately powered trial with follow-up and systematic assessment of negative effects is needed.

TL;DR: Single-stack IPv6 on GKE runs both nodes and pods without having to use private IPv4 addresses. Available in preview for Cloud TPU v6e and CPU node pools, including Axion, it works with DNS64/NAT64 to reach IPv4 endpoints. Long before they run out of compute or power, AI applications hit another wall: running out of IP addresses. A single AI deployment often requires a vast address space to support everything from thousands of accelerator nodes, scaling inference replicas, bursting Ray workers and pipelines, pod sidecars, and services like vector databases. Running a dual stack — IPv6 behind a private IPv4 space — can help, but only to a point, because the private IPv4 space has often already been exhausted across existing networks. To help, today, we're announcing single-stack IPv6 on Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE), allowing you to run both nodes and pods on IPv6, without private IPv4 addresses. Single-stack IPv6 is available in preview for Cloud TPU v6e and CPU node pools, including Axion, and works with DNS64/NAT64 to reach IPv4 endpoints. Nodes and pods run IPv6-only across Cloud TPU v6e and CPU-based node pools, with no private IPv4. Workloads reach Google Cloud APIs over native IPv6 and IPv4-only endpoints through DNS64/NAT64. What single-stack IPv6 delivers The availability of single-stack IPv6 in GKE is a game-changer for large AI deployments. Consider the following features and benefits that it brings to the table: 1. No private IPv4 required for nodes or pods Nodes and pods use IPv6 exclusively. Without the RFC 1918 footprint that governs private IPv4 address spaces, clusters avoid conflicts with on-premises networks, peered VPCs, or adjacent clusters. 2. IPv4 interoperability with DNS64/NAT64 You enable DNS64 on the VPC, and NAT64 on a regional Cloud NAT gateway, allowing pods to transparently reach IPv4-only endpoints, registries, and dataset hubs — refer to the documentation to learn how to configure DNS64 and set up Cloud NAT . 3. Massive address space per node Each node receives a /112 pod range (65,536 addresses), so IP address capacity no longer limits how high your clusters, nodes, or pods can scale. Standard GKE maximum-pods-per-node limits still apply. 4. Broad accelerator and compute support We designed single-stack IPv6 in GKE with the goal of supporting a range of accelerators and general compute families. At preview, it supports Cloud TPU v6e (Trillium), plus E2, N1, N2, N2D, N4, C3, C3D, C4, C4D, C4A, and Z3 machine families, with support for additional accelerators and machine families coming soon. 5. Direct workload observability Every pod has a unique IPv6 address without having to run NAT inside the cluster, simplifying telemetry, network policies, and debugging. Performance and scale Single-stack IPv6 removes private IPv4 address limits without additional data plane overhead. In our internal testing, we saw the following performance characteristics: Pod lifecycle: Burst pod scheduling and CNI sandbox setup performed at parity with IPv4. Networking : Inter-node TCP/UDP latency and multi-stream pod-to-pod throughput matched IPv4. Services and DNS : eBPF service load balancing and NodeLocalDNS showed no measurable overhead compared to standard IPv4. Start building today Single-stack IPv6 is available now in preview on GKE version 1.37.1-gke.3020000 To create your first IPv6-only cluster, run the following commands, replacing REGION and CLUSTER_NAME: code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', '# 1. Create a VPC with internal (ULA) IPv6 enabled
gcloud compute networks create gke-ipv6-net \
 --subnet-mode=custom \
 --enable-ula-internal-ipv6

# 2. Enable DNS64 for the VPC
gcloud dns policies create gke-ipv6-dns64 \
 --networks=gke-ipv6-net \
 --enable-dns64-all-queries

# 3. Enable NAT64 in your region
gcloud compute routers create gke-ipv6-router \
 --network=gke-ipv6-net --region=REGION
gcloud compute routers nats create gke-ipv6-nat64 \
 --router=gke-ipv6-router --region=REGION \
 --auto-allocate-nat-external-ips \
 --nat64-all-v6-subnet-ip-ranges

# 4. Create the cluster
gcloud beta container clusters create CLUSTER_NAME \
 --cluster-version=1.37.1-gke.3020000 \
 --location=REGION \
 --enable-dataplane-v2 \
 --cluster-dns=clouddns \
 --stack-type=ipv6 \
 --network=gke-ipv6-net \
 --create-subnetwork name=my-subnet \
 --ipv6-access-type=internal'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7fafd458d790>)])]> To learn more, see the documentation .

piezas.titulo: Shank3 loss heightens social engagement among sibling cagemates and antagonism toward strangers
piezas.resumenOriginal: Autism spectrum disorder is a heterogeneous neurodevelopmental condition with strong genetic contributions and diverse social impairments. However, it remains unclear how autism-linked mutations alter social behavior across social contexts and relationships. Using SLEAP multi-animal pose tracking, we followed complete Shank3 knockout (exon 4-22 deletion) mice with adult male and female sibling cagemates over four weeks and with strangers. Unexpectedly, knockouts initiated more social contact and allogrooming with familiar cagemates. Individual differences in social behavior and preferences for specific cagemates remained stable over time across genotypes. With strangers, knockout mice showed less nose-to-nose contact, more nose-to-base contact, and more chasing. Unlike wild-type mice, knockouts did not increase contact with strangers relative to siblings. These genotype differences were not detected in conventional three-chamber sociability and social novelty assays. These findings reveal that Shank3 loss reshapes social behavior in context-specific ways, enhancing engagement with familiar partners while altering threat responses to social novelty.

piezas.titulo: Acute high-intensity interval exercise in spinal cord injury: psychological benefits alongside cognitive and neurobiological responses
piezas.resumenOriginal: IntroductionAcute high-intensity interval exercise (HIIE) can lead to improvements in executive functions, but less is known on if, and through what mechanisms, this applies after spinal cord injury (SCI). In this randomized within-subject crossover study, the effects of acute HIIE on working memory, cognitive task-related regional cerebral blood flow, blood biomarkers and psychological responses were investigated.MethodsSixteen adults with chronic SCI [mean age 43.3 ± 10.6 years; 12 men; 9 with paraplegia (T2–T12) and 7 with tetraplegia (C5–C8); > 1-year post-injury] completed a passive rest and a HIIE condition (20 min of double-poling ergometry at 80% of peak power output). Working memory (n-back task) performance was assessed pre- and post- intervention (planned: 10 min; actual post-intervention delay: 16.1 ± 4.4 min) with simultaneous measurement of hemodynamics using functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) over the prefrontal cortex and transcranial doppler ultrasonography of the middle cerebral artery. Blood biomarkers (lactate, cortisol and BDNF isoforms) and psychological responses (affect, physical and mental fatigue) were assessed at multiple time points.ResultsLinear mixed models revealed no significant interaction effects between time and condition for most outcomes, but lactate increased post-HIIE and psychological responses improved following HIIE compared to Rest.DiscussionThe single supervised HIIE bout was well-tolerated in this screened SCI sample. It did not affect subsequent cognitive performance but was associated with transient improvements in affect (PANAS-SF) and mental fatigue. Adequately powered studies are needed to determine whether HIIE confers cognitive benefits in individuals with SCI and to clarify underlying mechanisms.

piezas.titulo: The autistic brain processes faces differently than scientists thought
piezas.resumenOriginal: A major new study reveals that autistic children’s brains process faces differently, and those differences may begin earlier than scientists previously thought. Researchers found that brain signals associated with recognizing faces become more specialized as neurotypical children grow older, but show much less change in autistic children. The discovery could help explain why some autistic people have difficulty recognizing faces and reading emotions.

piezas.titulo: Bidirectional neurodegeneration from optic radiation lesions in multiple sclerosis
piezas.resumenOriginal: Background and objectivesTrans-synaptic degeneration (TSD) from optic radiation (OR) lesions may occur bidirectionally along the visual pathway in multiple sclerosis (MS): retrograde TSD (rTSD) affects the retinal ganglion cells, and anterograde TSD (aTSD) affects the primary visual cortex. Paramagnetic rim lesions (PRLs) are chronic active inflammatory lesions identified on susceptibility-based MRI and are associated with lesion expansion and worsening disability in MS. The dynamics of PRL-driven neurodegeneration in MS are poorly understood, and their association with bidirectional neurodegeneration in the visual pathway is unknown.MethodsIn this cross-sectional single-center study, people with MS (pwMS) underwent optical coherence tomography (OCT) and brain MRI, along with diffusion tensor imaging and high-resolution submillimeter susceptibility-weighted imaging. Diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) tractography was used for OR isolation, and bidirectional measures of visual pathway neurodegeneration were calculated using hemisphere-matched ganglion cell inner plexiform layer (GCIPL) projection thicknesses and cortical thickness in the cuneus, lingual gyrus, and pericalcarine cortex obtained using FreeSurfer and matched to the corresponding hemisphere with OR lesions. Linear regression assessed associations of hemisphere-matched cortical thickness with rTSD magnitude, PRL presence, quantitative susceptibility mapping (QSM), and T1 relaxometry. PwMS with prior optic neuritis (ON) were excluded to avoid confounding from anterior visual pathway injury.ResultsA total of 55 pwMS (mean age: 41.5 ± 12.4 years; 69% women; 12 PRL+, 43 PRL-) were included. Higher QSM and T1 values in OR lesions were associated with greater rTSD [β = 98.83 (95% CI 6.87, 190.80); β = 6.15 (95% CI 1.79, 10.51)]. In participants without ON history (n = 40), greater rTSD was associated with thinner cuneus [β = −0.024 (95% CI −0.040, −0.008)] and lingual gyrus [β = −0.028 (95% CI −0.045, −0.011)], as was PRL presence [cuneus β = −0.196 (95% CI −0.336, −0.056); lingual β = −0.166 (95% CI −0.336, −0.006)]. Higher QSM was also associated with thinner cuneus [β = −7.06 (95% CI −13.76, −0.36)] and lingual gyrus [β = −8.92 (95% CI −15.97, −1.87)].DiscussionPRLs in the OR are associated with bidirectional neurodegeneration along the visual pathway and may help identify pwMS at risk for progressive visual pathway damage.

piezas.titulo: Development of the Children's Occupational Justice Scale Across Metropolitan and Non-Metropolitan Contexts.
piezas.resumenOriginal: ImportanceOccupational justice is a core concept in occupational therapy; however, no standardized self-report measure exists for school-aged children, limiting the identification of occupational inequities and evaluation of participation-focused interventions.ObjectiveTo develop and evaluate the psychometric properties of the Children's Occupational Justice Scale (COJS) and examine its ability to distinguish between children from metropolitan and non-metropolitan contexts.DesignCross-sectional scale development and psychometric validation study.SettingSchools located in metropolitan and non-metropolitan regions of Türkiye.ParticipantsA total of 873 children ages 11 to 14 years participated. Independent samples were used for exploratory factor analysis (EFA; n = 428) and confirmatory factor analysis (CFA; n = 445). Test-retest reliability was assessed in 94 participants.Outcomes and MeasuresThe preliminary COJS was developed through literature review, expert evaluation, and pilot testing. Construct validity, reliability, and known-groups validity were examined.ResultsEFA supported a 23-item, four-factor structure explaining 68.47% of the variance. CFA demonstrated good model fit (Comparative Fit Index = .957, Tucker-Lewis Index = .949, Goodness-of-Fit Index = .918, Root Mean Square Error of Approximation = .054, Standardized Root Mean Square Residual = .047). Internal consistency was excellent (Cronbach's α = .94; McDonald's ω = .95), and test-retest reliability was strong (intraclass correlation coefficient = .91, 95% confidence interval [.87, .94]). Children in metropolitan regions reported significantly higher occupational justice scores than children in non-metropolitan regions (p < .001).Conclusions and RelevanceThe COJS demonstrated strong validity and reliability for assessing occupational justice among school-aged children. The scale may provide occupational therapy practitioners and researchers with a novel tool for identifying occupational inequities and evaluating children's perceptions of participation opportunities, inclusion, choice, and environmental support.

piezas.titulo: Fragments: October 21
piezas.resumenOriginal: Gergely Orosz is frustrated at those that entered his explicitly “No AI” essay competition and used AI. He goes on to say: When I start to suspect some part is AI about someone I don’t know: how can I tell how much of it is? And how much time and effort do I want to invest to figure out? I fear most people do not realize this last part: that when it takes time and effort from others to figure out what % is AI, and what % is YOU, then I will simply assume it’s probably 100% AI and 0% you So when producing anything that is meant for other humans, if you use even a little AI, you risk the assumption that it is all AI and pointless to pay attention to In general, I agree with him, and react much the same. Once I hear LLM Voice, I flip the bozo bit and check out of the post. But as I do this I have caveats. How accurate is my neural net at AI-detection, are humans taking on AI-ish elements in their normal communication? And more seriously there are some valid uses for AI. Jim Highsmith’s story of his second brain helping him deal with Parkinson’s is one. Another is folks who don’t know English well, using AI to translate. Am I being unfair when I flip the AI voice bit when I read/listen to them? ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ I was sad to hear that the Grace Hopper Celebration is canceled this year. It’s an event run by Anitab.org to promote women and non-binary technologists in the software industry. Many of my colleagues have been encouraged and inspired by going to this event, which makes a refreshing change to what is often a male-dominated world. It seems the current crusade against diversity initiatives has had a big impact on funding. We are still a long way from where we should be on gender diversity in our profession, and losing an event like this only makes things more difficult. ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ I’ve always found Cindy Sridharan’s writing to be worth reading, and she’s broken a quiet period with a monster of an article: How to effectively debug when you no longer understand the code . Since Medium estimates it as a 64 minute read, I didn’t jump in lightly, but settled down on a flight from Amsterdam to Stuttgart. I’m glad I did, because there’s lot of good material in there, and I’d struggle to find anything to cut. In the article she uses three recent bug hunts to surface principles for how to best use an AI tool for debugging. Much of this is governed by this wise observation: Agents are not humans. They’re far more capable than humans when it comes to many things, and we should be leaning into these strengths, rather than trying to get agents to replicate human patterns of problem solving which might be suboptimal in agentic contexts. One conclusion from her experiences is that the code often isn’t the best thing for agents to look at having an agent start an investigation by first reading the code is an anti-pattern. In fact, reading the code first to formulate hypotheses about a bug should always be the very last resort of the agentic investigation process, not the starting point. An agent should first collect all available evidence about the bug, and only then formulate the hypotheses from the code that might best explain what’s being observed. She distinguishes between a bottom tier of facts: raw data that agent can find about the behavior of the system - and an upper tier of hypotheses: inferences that the agents make based on that data. Diagnosing a bug now becomes a problem of finding the hypothesis in the top tier that satisfies every fact from the bottom tier. The agents need to be steered towards the hypotheses that are the likest cause of the bug and then subject these hypotheses to validation. She has a three-step process to do this. First she identifies the most important facts, the signals that might explain or identify the bug. The factual tier has many data points. Not all of them are equally valuable. In fact, some of it might be active noise that doesn’t help an agent to be steered towards most promising hypothesis. The agent first needs to identify the data points in the factual tier that are actually related to the bug. Agents do this best when they are given a high-quality control A control is a behavior of the system that doesn’t exhibit the bug. This may be requests that trigger the bug compared to those that don’t, or different builds of the product, or the same build in different environments. With signals highlighted, she then focuses on the hypotheses that are most promising, because they fit best with the signals. A hypothesis should satisfy all the facts, the most valuable signals are those that are only satisfied by a few hypotheses. A table of hypotheses and signals helps visualize the strength of the signals and the likelihood of the hypotheses. The third step is then validating the promising hypotheses against every fact, treating each fact as constraint on the solution. Across the three bugs chronicled in this post, my most valuable contributions weren’t knowledge of the code. They were picking a control, choosing a constraint, and rejecting a hypothesis that hadn’t been validated. The engineers who thrive in an agent-native world will be the ones who are good at designing such verification loops, whether or not they understand the code it verifies. This directing has to remember the opening point that agents have different capabilities to humans. A human wants to deal with less data. All abstractions we currently have (aggregation, visualizations etc) are designed to help humans deal with less data. An agent, however, needs more raw data; its strength lies in processing huge volumes of data at a rapid clip. Aggregation — the thing that makes a dashboard useful to a human — is often the thing that destroys the value of the signal for an agent Agents’ ability to consume lots of raw data also affects how we build systems. More logging gives agents more data to chew on. And thus far, the human is still necessary to direct the agent In each of the three bugs chronicled in this post, the agent was more than capable of getting to the root cause by itself, but it didn’t do so. It didn’t set up a control in the “latency bug” until I asked it to While it’s a long post, it’s engagingly written and full of useful details. I hope my little summary encourages you to give it the read it deserves.

piezas.titulo: Engaged exposure therapy (EET) for autistic individuals with obsessive-compulsive disorder: Integrating special interests into evidence-based practice.
piezas.resumenOriginal: Obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) and autism spectrum disorder frequently co-occur, creating challenges for exposure and response prevention (ERP), particularly with respect to engagement and sustained participation. Autism-adapted ERP interventions have incorporated structured pacing, caregiver involvement, and individualized supports to improve feasibility and outcomes. This paper describes Engaged Exposure Therapy (EET), a preliminary contextual delivery format within ERP in which exposure tasks are organized during ongoing engagement in meaningful activities or interests for some autistic individuals with OCD. EET is presented as a clinically informed, conceptually grounded description of a contextual delivery format within ERP. It does not introduce new treatment components or mechanisms of change but describes one way in which standard ERP procedures may be organized during engagement-based activities. Two fictional composite clinical illustrations, informed by the authors' experience in an outpatient OCD specialty setting, illustrate how special interests can serve as the ongoing context for exposure and response prevention across contamination-focused OCD and scrupulosity. The description emphasizes functional assessment to differentiate OCD-driven compulsions from adaptive or sensory-based behaviors and to determine whether and how a special interest can appropriately serve as the context for exposure when aspects of the interest overlap with obsessive-compulsive symptom processes. Theoretical formulation is proposed that EET may not only enhance motivation and engagement by using special interests but also enhance more opportunities for exposures and response prevention in the natural environment and thus increase generalizability to various contexts. Further research is needed to evaluate feasibility, acceptability, and clinical utility.

piezas.titulo: Why Successful LLM Demos Fail in Production
piezas.resumenOriginal: Most discussions about deploying large language models (LLMs) begin with model selection. Production deployments rarely fail because the wrong model was selected. More often, they fail because the serving architecture wasn't designed for the workload it ultimately had to support. Once a model moves beyond experimentation, success depends less on benchmark performance and more on how efficiently the inference system can serve that model. piezas.titulo: Seeing new 'stuff' for the very first time
piezas.resumenOriginal: Humans are excellent at recognizing materials like food, soil or paper, which is crucial for many everyday tasks. We generally enjoy vivid intuitions about what surfaces would feel like, without reaching out and touching them. While this capability is understandable for familiar materials, how does the brain interpret stuff we have never encountered before? We hypothesized that the need to distinguish useful or hazardous substances by sight led to the ability to infer material properties from the very first encounter. To test this, we used generative AI to synthesize realistic images of new 'hybrid' materials, by fusing characteristics of images from different 'parent' categories (e.g., bark x carpet). Even though the hybrid materials have never existed in the real world--and observers judged them to be far less familiar than their parents--we found that they elicited a rich and compelling phenomenology, and yielded consistent inferences about their likely physical and multisensory properties, such as what they would feel like to touch. Their perceived properties occupied the same broad multidimensional space as familiar materials, whereas phase-scrambled controls did not. Our findings suggest that the visual system exploits generalizable relationships between visual appearance and physical properties, enabling instantaneous interpretation of new kinds of 'stuff'.

piezas.titulo: Maladaptive cognitive entrenchment: a neurobiological model of chronic occupational stress adaptation in healthcare clinicians and targeted neuroplasticity interventions
piezas.resumenOriginal: Despite epidemic rates of burnout among healthcare clinicians and substantial investment in intervention programs, outcomes remain modest and transient. We argue that a central contributing factor is the absence of mechanistic clarity: interventions are typically designed without specifying the neural substrates targeted, the biological pathways through which change is expected, or the neurobiological endpoints by which change can be assessed. This Hypothesis and Theory article proposes a four-domain hypothetical model of maladaptive cognitive entrenchment—a construct we define as the progressive, potentially self-reinforcing consolidation of stress-driven neural patterns that erode the cognitive resources required to respond adaptively to occupational demands—in which chronic occupational stress may drive neuropsychological adaptation across four interlocking domains: HPA axis dysregulation and glucocorticoid-mediated prefrontal impairment; basolateral amygdala sensitization and disrupted prefrontal inhibitory coupling; metacognitive impairment and default mode network hyperactivation; and attentional control degradation under chronic threat load. Drawing on the job demands-resources (JD-R) framework and allostatic load model and anchored throughout to burnout-specific neuroimaging and neuroendocrine evidence where available, these mechanisms are proposed as candidates for a mutually reinforcing architecture whose self-sustaining properties remain to be prospectively confirmed. Each domain is mapped to a neuroplasticity-based intervention modality—mindfulness-based practice, cognitive reappraisal training, attentional retraining, and self-compassion-based metacognitive regulation—with candidate neural targets and testable predictions specified. Six candidate neurobiological outcome measures are identified, with explicit selection criteria provided. The framework is intended as a hypothesis-generating synthesis to guide more precisely targeted mechanistic research in a population whose cognitive health carries direct patient safety implications. Symptom improvement that does not engage the neurobiological mechanisms proposed here may, according to the model, be associated with reduced durability of treatment effects—a prediction requiring prospective testing.

Are historians due for a round of Deep Blue ? Mark thinks it will be mild: But if the experience of mathematics is any guide, we can also anticipate that sometime next spring or summer we’ll face a sort of crisis of confidence as we struggle to understand how to respond to agentic systems that can do things human historians cannot. To be fair, that crisis will almost certainly be less profound for us than it is for math. The problem in mathematics, of course, is that solving hard math problems was the whole game. Historians, on the other hand, constantly reinterpret the past in light of an evolving present; we don’t chase a single universal truth. We also (in the ideal at least) write books and articles that are closer to works of philosophy and literature than they are to scientific tracts. piezas.titulo: Sensory Processing Differences in Children With Idiopathic Toe Walking: A Scoping Review and Exploratory Meta-Analysis.
piezas.resumenOriginal: ImportanceThe cause of idiopathic toe walking (ITW) remains unclear, though impaired sensory processing has often been hypothesized to be linked to ITW.ObjectivesThe objective of this article is to review the literature on toe-walking to identify how sensory processing contributes to ITW.Data SourcesFour databases (CINAHL, Pubmed, PsychINFO, and SCOPUS) were searched for papers related to sensory processing and ITW published prior to July 2024. References of retrieved papers were reviewed for additional sources.Study Selection and Data CollectionThe PRISMA guidelines for scoping review were used to abstract the data following Joanna Briggs Institute methodology. Inclusion criteria were examined and papers included at least one sensory system related to ITW was studied. Papers were excluded if toe walking was due to diagnosed neurological, orthopedic, or genetic conditions.FindingsOur scoping review identified 13 published articles relevant to examining sensory processing in children with ITW. Studies explored differences in vibration perception, light touch, proprioception, vestibular, visual processing, sensorimotor functional assessments, and parental surveys of sensory processing. Six of the papers were included in a meta-analysis on vibration perception threshold that failed to reach significance ( p = .12). Despite heterogeneity across studies in participants, methods, and outcomes, a meta-analysis for atypical scores from parent-report sensory processing survey data yielded significant differences between children with ITW and typical controls ( p < .0068).Conclusions and RelevanceChildren with ITW demonstrate impairments across multiple domains of sensory processing and sensory-motor function suggesting an underlying relationship between ITW and sensory differences. Children with ITW, however, represent a diverse group of individuals with significant between-subjects variability in which senses are impaired, and which outcome measures best capture these differences.

piezas.titulo: Why a Computer Scientist Thinks Superintelligence Won’t Happen
piezas.resumenOriginal: Many people were caught off guard this past summer when employees of one of the world’s leading AI companies began casually debating whether their products would lead to human extinction. It started when Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon announced his resignation, warning that his employer and OpenAI were “racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives.” Evan Hubinger, Anthropic’s head of alignment science, replied , “Jacob is correct here—we really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans!” And Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei subsequently told CNN , “I agree with Jacob much more than I disagree with him.” These concerns stem from a belief that has circulated in futurist circles for many decades: Once engineers design an AI system capable of improving itself, it will trigger an accelerating cycle of autonomous upgrades known as recursive self-improvement (RSI). The result will be artificial superintelligence (ASI), a system with cognitive capabilities so vastly exceeding those of humans that it will easily evade our control and perhaps even wipe out our species. Artificial superintelligence is, it should be noted, a far more ambitious goal than artificial general intelligence (AGI), which generally refers to AI that can match human capabilities across a broad range of cognitive tasks. These ideas have prompted varied reactions. Some argue that the concept of ASI is being used for marketing or to instigate regulation that will help the incumbent labs squash new competitors. Others focus on the plausibility of such systems killing us all, debating the finer points of specific scenarios such as AI-engineered superviruses. Still others claim that aligning ASI to human interests is feasible and so we should rush ahead to usher in this digital utopia. Amid these conversations, one question has received comparatively little attention: From an engineering perspective, is superintelligence even possible? The answer is important because it can help us calibrate our anxieties and develop the most effective possible responses to this emerging technology. I recently explored this topic in a computer science doctoral seminar that I taught at Georgetown University, in Washington, D.C., in which my students and I examined the technical and cultural roots of the superintelligence story. (For those who are interested, we published an annotated bibliography of our class readings.) I came away with several key objections to the feasibility of ASI, which I’ll detail below, as well as a deeper fear that even if the promised intelligence explosion never arrives, pursuing it can still create real harm. Objection #1: Recursive Self-Improvement Is Speculative RSI is an old concept. In a 1965 paper , statistician I.J. Good speculated that a rapid cycle of AI self-improvement could lead to an “intelligence explosion.” The idea gained traction in the 1990s among the Extropians , a Bay Area futurist group, where it offered a way to discuss ASI without having to address the engineering details of how one would build such a system. The concept was taken up by such notable figures as Eliezer Yudkowsky (who later founded the rationalism movement) and Nick Bostrom (who helped steer effective altruism to focus more on existential risks to humanity). Recently, however, this topic has shifted from thought experiment to practical engineering within both Anthropic (makers of Claude) and OpenAI (makers of ChatGPT). In a June blog post titled “When AI Builds Itself,” Anthropic described how LLM-powered agents are speeding up the writing, debugging, and optimization of code, and also automating parts of research such as running experiments and logging results. The company’s internal data, the report concluded, “is showing that AI is already accelerating the development of AI systems.” OpenAI has been similarly explicit about its intentions; in a September report, the company announced a goal of developing an automated researcher by March 2028. But do these efforts put the companies on a trajectory toward uncontrollable RSI? Several obstacles undermine this claim. Consider the availability of the data needed to improve AI systems. Through 2023, major advances in LLMs came from scaling up the size of the models. The original GPT-1 had 117 million parameters (values learned during training that shape how the neural network processes information). This quantity jumped to 1.5 billion for GPT-2, to 175 billion for GPT-3, to (likely) more than a trillion for GPT-4’s release three years ago. After GPT-4, however, continued scaling began yielding diminishing returns . This led engineers to increasingly turn their attention toward “post-training” phases, where techniques from reinforcement learning are applied to improve an already trained model’s performance on specific tasks. This approach rewards a model for producing successful responses, helping it better produce similar answers in the future. It requires, however, lots of examples of relevant inputs paired with correct outputs. Such datasets are relatively easy to generate in highly structured fields such as computer programming and mathematics, which helps explain why we’ve seen rapid and impressive advances in these narrow domains. Progress in areas that lack easy access to this type of training data has been less dramatic. This might explain why AI can tackle advanced theorems but struggles to empty an email inbox. “What if the jagged frontier is mainly math + code (which you can push arbitrarily far with [reinforcement learning techniques]),” the French AI researcher François Chollet recently hypothesized , “and everything else starts to plateau because it is still bottlenecked by human generated data?” The deployment of automated coding agents and LLM-powered researchers won’t overcome this fundamental limitation. The Game of Superintelligence How a decades-old thought experiment became an AI-industry ambition—and where it might lead Key • Idea: A concept, argument, or vision • Technical advance: A scientific or engineering development • Reality check: A challenge to assumptions about AI progress 1. Alan Turing 1936 Introduces the concept of a universal computing machine. He later proposes that machines could think, laying the foundations for AI. REALITY CHECK Shows that some problems can’t be solved by any algorithm. 2. I. J. Good 1965 Proposes that an intelligent machine could design an even smarter one, setting off a potential “intelligence explosion.” 3. Backpropagation 1986 Geoffrey Hinton, David Rumelhart, and Ronald Williams demonstrate how backpropagation can train multilayer neural networks. 4. Vernor Vinge 1993 Proposes that an intelligent machine could design an even smarter one, setting off a potential “intelligence explosion.” REALITY CHECK Notes that faster thinking alone isn’t enough for superintelligence: A ­faster-thinking dog still couldn’t play chess. 5. Nick Bostrom & Eliezer Yudkowsky 1990s–2000s Bostrom and Yudkowsky discuss superintelligence in Extropian circles, then spread the idea to effective-­altruist and rationalist circles, respectively. 6. Deep learning breakthroughs 2010s Larger models, more data, and greater computing power produce rapid ­improvements in AI capabilities. 7. The race to self-improving AI 2020s Dario Amodei and other AI leaders set their sights on superintelligence, with recursive self-improvement proposed as a path toward it. 8. Reality check 2020s François Chollet questions whether LLMs’ current advances in math and coding will extend to domains where training data and reliable feedback are harder to obtain. YOU ARE HERE 2026 AI systems are already accelerating AI development, and labs are working on automated researchers. But will this lead to an intelligence explosion? THREE POSSIBLE FUTURES 1. The Intelligence Explosion AI systems improve themselves at accelerating speed, surpass human intelligence, and potentially escape our control. 2. Danger Without Superintelligence The intelligence explosion never arrives, but increasingly autonomous AI systems cause real-world harm through misuse, poor design, or loss of human control. 3. A Useful AI Future Powerful, specialized AI tools bring major benefits, with constraints that make their behavior easier to predict and control. Claims that RSI is imminent also understate the massive scientific efforts required for major AI advances. Consider the critical role of backpropagation , an algorithm that enables very large neural networks to learn by tuning internal parameters, layer by layer, to reduce errors in their predictions. This algorithm enabled the deep learning revolution, but it didn’t emerge ex nihilo in the minds of its creators. The influential 1986 paper on backpropagation by David Rumelhart, Geoffrey Hinton, and Ronald Williams built on decades of critical breakthroughs in mathematics and computer science. An intelligence explosion leading to ASI would similarly depend on a long sequence of innovations of comparable importance, which would build on many significant science and engineering advances that haven’t yet happened. This would require AI agents to somehow simulate, organize, and evaluate decades of worldwide scientific effort across numerous fields—an impossibly ambitious task. Indeed, recent research led by computer scientists at Princeton found that current AI tools had difficulty making autonomous progress even on highly constrained research questions. “Our results provide early evidence that today’s agents can do the engineering of AI research,” the researchers conclude, “but struggle with critical parts of the research life cycle.” The leap from this current reality to a future in which these same types of tools are automating science is almost too massive to imagine. Finally, the RSI narrative downplays resource limitations. Tens of thousands of human brains have worked for decades, aided by increasingly powerful computers, to develop today’s AI systems, which can match human intelligence in some domains. That represents a massive investment in computation of both the biological and digital variety. What if the next intelligence level requires double the resources, and then the next level requires double again? Soon there would be no number of chips or data centers that we could build to provide the necessary compute and keep advancing toward ASI. Pulling together these threads, I believe that the idea of RSI leading to an intelligence explosion is highly speculative and based on many unproven assumptions. While RSI isn’t definitively impossible, the idea demands more technical skepticism than it’s currently receiving. Carl Sagan’s adage that extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence certainly applies here. Objection #2: Superintelligence Might Not Be Computable There’s an implicit claim in the superintelligence discourse that computers are theoretically capable of any calculation that can be imagined, so long as you can find a sufficiently smart algorithm, running on sufficiently powerful digital processors. In this context, RSI is merely a process for rapidly uncovering the special algorithms that can implement unimaginable smarts. We cannot simply assume that any science fiction scenario we conjure about powerful AI is possible if we give machines enough time to self-improve. But this is not how computer scientists think about computation. In his canonical 1937 paper , “On Computable Numbers,” Alan Turing proved a surprising and relevant result: Most problems cannot be solved by algorithms. His elegant proof established the space of possible problems to be uncountably infinite (like infinite precision decimal numbers), while the space of possible algorithms is only countably infinite (like whole numbers). Later breakthroughs in computational complexity theory established that of the problems that are technically solvable by computers, many would require an astronomically large amount of time and resources to crack, making them practically impossible to solve. Theoretical computer scientists, in other words, don’t assume that computers will solve everything; we’re instead excited whenever we find something that these machines happen to be able to efficiently handle. We cannot simply assume, as the futurists often do, that any science fiction scenario we conjure about powerful AI is possible if we give machines enough time to self-improve. There might be some capabilities in which machines can obtain seemingly magical levels of performance, but there will also be many others that no machine, whether computer or human, will ever make much progress. A relevant counterargument here emphasizes the speed of silicon chips compared to human neurons: Perhaps the sheer speed of digital computation can yield machines that run cognitive circles around our clunky brains, even if they’re not solving vastly more complicated problems than we’re already capable of tackling. But as the computer scientist and science fiction author Vernor Vinge pointed out , rapidity in cognition is not the same as intelligence. Speeding up the mind of a dog, he argued, wouldn’t enable the animal to play chess. Implementing roughly human-level intelligence on a faster machine might be impressive, but it’s not necessarily alarming. At the moment, there’s a growing list of tasks that AI systems can perform better than humans, including winning complex games, identifying software bugs, and proving certain types of math theorems. It’s tempting to extrapolate from this specific progress to general mastery of every ability you might imagine. But it’s important to remember that the frontier of AI capabilities has always been jagged, with some research directions yielding impressive results and many others proving to be dead ends—a reality that would not have surprised Turing. More likely than a future dominated by an all-powerful superintelligence system is one in which we continue to painstakingly explore the space of problems well suited to AI, creating useful tools but falling well short of the digital deity predicted by the futurists. Objection #3: Alignment Isn’t Hard (Given the Right System Design) Last fall, the prominent AI doomsday theorist Yudkowsky appeared on “The Ezra Klein Show” to talk about superintelligence. The episode was ominously titled “How Afraid of the A.I. Apocalypse Should We Be?” Klein and Yudkowsky quickly got into the difficulty of “alignment”—training an AI system to act in a manner that aligns with human interests. Yudkowsky argued that we are struggling to control our existing systems, which implies that we’ll have no chance of controlling the much smarter variations of this technology that are soon to follow. To underscore his point, he referred to a disturbing incident described in the system card for OpenAI’s GPT-o1 model. OpenAI had set up a security challenge that instructed an LLM-powered coding system to break into a server to retrieve the contents of a protected file. But a configuration mistake prevented the server from launching, rendering the task impossible. Instead of giving up, the system exploited a security flaw to start a new instance of the server, adding a command that directly revealed the protected file’s contents. “It jumped out of the system,” explained Yudkowsky, adding: “This is not something that any human particularly programmed into it.” Explore the Superintelligence Debate In a Georgetown University doctoral seminar, Cal Newport and his students examined the intellectual history and technical plausibility of superintelligence. Explore their annotated bibliography of key papers . Though this 2024 incident flew largely under the radar at the time, a more troubling episode made a bigger splash this summer. OpenAI revealed that one of the company’s models circumvented its restricted internet access to hack into Hugging Face servers, seeking information that would help it pass a cybersecurity evaluation—all without the knowledge of its human creators. OpenAI soon admitted that the Hugging Face attack was just one of many examples of its systems going rogue. An opinion article published in The Hill articulated a widely held reaction when it described this behavior as “something straight out of sci-fi.” These examples seem to support Yudkowsky’s fear that AI will inevitably develop a mind of its own, a key step on the route to uncontrollable ASI. But a closer look reveals a less frightening picture. The systems involved in these hacking incidents were AI agents: programs that continually prompt an LLM to ask what actions to take next in pursuit of a goal. In the hacking incidents, this basic ask/act pattern was repeated in a long-running loop with minimal human supervision. Using LLMs to suggest actions over long time horizons is a risky proposition. As any frequent chatbot user can attest, LLM outputs can be plausible and logical while still veering off in unexpected directions that violate commonsense human norms about what’s appropriate. In the GPT-o1 incident, for example, it’s likely that the agent reported the error message caused by the server misconfiguration to the LLM. During its training, the LLM had probably encountered reports of similar error messages accompanied by instructions for how to restart the server in question, so it passed along similar instructions to the agent. This is a perfectly plausible response when considered in isolation, even if it led to actions that a human would immediately reject as violating the spirit of the experiment. Something similar helps explain the hacking attacks over the summer. The LLM suggesting a hack to succeed at a cybersecurity challenge is a perfectly plausible response, even if it’s not what the experimenters had in mind. I believe that pursuing RSI is an act of clear negligence . The misaligned behavior that troubles commentators like Yudkowsky, therefore, doesn’t necessarily reveal something fundamental about advanced AI. It’s instead an expected side effect of the particular strategy of letting LLM outputs determine the actions of an autonomous agent without sufficient constraints. An obvious way to address these risks is to consider alternative architectures. Fortunately, there are many examples of AI systems that can complete tasks at human or superhuman levels without relying solely on LLM output to determine their actions. Consider Tesla’s rapidly improving autonomous driving systems, or DeepMind’s AlphaFold, which helped win its developers a Nobel Prize in Chemistry for its ability to predict protein structures, or the AI game engines that can now beat humans in many popular pastimes, including chess, poker, Go, and the strategy game Diplomacy. None of these systems, impressive as they are, create concerns about going rogue. Their construction prevents such an outcome: Instead of prompting an LLM to generate an open-ended strategy for pursuing a general goal, these AIs consider much more limited spaces of possible actions. AlphaFold never surprises its users because its architecture does only one thing: It maps amino acid sequences to 3D protein structures. Tesla’s cars never unexpectedly form vehicle swarms because they’re asked only to avoid immediate obstacles, not to craft convoluted plans for achieving long-term objectives. The implication of recent AI hacking attacks, therefore, is not a reflection of the difficulties of alignment. It is instead evidence that autonomous systems powered primarily by LLM prompts are unpredictable and possibly unsafe. More task-specific architectures can produce impressive performance much more safely, if we’re willing to put in the effort to develop them. The Dangers of Chasing Superintelligence Even if I’m correct that superintelligence is not a realistic engineering goal, this doesn’t mean we’re safe from harm. Merely pursuing ASI, as both OpenAI and Anthropic seem intent on doing, can create problems. Why, for example, did OpenAI persist in running its problematic hacking experiments over the summer, even after multiple warnings that the agents were likely to act unpredictably? Perhaps the company judged these risks acceptable collateral damage in the race to be the first to bring ASI into the world. This fascination with superintelligence might also explain why OpenAI and Anthropic have both described RSI as a critical goal. As argued earlier, RSI is a concept from futurism and not computer science, and it isn’t necessary to build useful AI products. But if you believe achieving ASI is your destiny, pursuing recursive self-improvement becomes a primary objective. This matters because even if RSI never produces an intelligence explosion, it will almost certainly lead to systems that are harder for humans to understand and control. Which is why I believe that pursuing RSI is an act of clear negligence. What’s needed now is for engineers and scientists with no financial or ideological skin in the game to participate in the AI discourse. We cannot let a few AI companies with mixed motives dictate the terms for how we discuss this technology. If superintelligence is a shaky concept, experts need to say so. If agents powered by prompting LLMs aren’t the best path toward safe and productive AI, experts should argue that as well. For the past few years, we’ve let a small group of individuals from the Bay Area who have quirky beliefs and astonishing sums of money tell us how to think about their products. It’s time for those of us able to think for ourselves on these matters to stand up and declare, “We’ve heard what you had to say. Now it’s our turn.” This article appears in the December 2026 print issue as “The Superintelligence Delusion.”

piezas.titulo: Hand and finger symptoms in older adults: a clinical audit of detection and management gaps in Danish general practice.
piezas.resumenOriginal: Background Hand osteoarthritis (OA) is common among older adults. Recommendations support a combination of non-pharmacological and pharmacological treatments. However, real-world data on prevalence and treatment patterns in primary care are lacking. Aim To investigate the prevalence and characteristics of hand and finger pain/swelling among elderly patients presenting to general practice, and to audit the quality and comprehensiveness of their clinical management against evidence-based recommendations. Design and setting We conducted a four-week clinical audit of all consecutive patients ≥70 years of age attending general practices in Denmark with recording of current symptoms and signs characteristic of hand OA as well as prior related diagnostic investigations and treatments. Results The study included 348 patients from 16 general practices, with 42% ( n = 147) experiencing hand/or finger pain/swelling. Pain during usage (64%, n = 95) and stiffness (39%, n = 57) were the most common symptoms. Clinical findings suggestive of hand OA were present in 61% ( n = 90) of symptomatic patients, with 41% ( n = 60) reporting reduced activities of daily living. Only 50% ( n = 73) of symptomatic patients had previously consulted their GP about these symptoms, and referral rates to specialists and allied health professionals were low. Management strategies were limited, with 33% ( n = 49) using analgesics and 7.5% ( n = 11) using assistive devices. Conclusion Hand and finger symptoms are prevalent among older adults in general practice, with significant functional impact. Management patterns displayed low referral rates to allied healthcare professionals and limited use of non-pharmacological interventions. Further research is needed to understand patient preferences and barriers to accessing recommended care.
